caption: The star cluster M23 in Sagittarius, imaged by the Burrell Schmidt telescope at Kitt Peak
story: Stars crowd this frame, broken here and there by black patches where no background stars shine through, while one bright star stands out at the upper right. This is M23, also listed as NGC 6494, a large, bright and richly populated star cluster in the constellation Sagittarius.

M23 lies some 2200 light-years from us and measures about 20 light-years across, which on the sky covers roughly 30 arcminutes; the whole picture is 35 arcminutes wide. The cluster is thought to be more than 200 million years old. That bright star at the upper right is not a member at all: it sits in the foreground, between us and the cluster.

Because M23 lies in the plane of our Galaxy, light from stars farther away has to pass through dust on its way here. The dust makes those background stars look progressively redder, and where it is thickest it hides them completely, producing the dark gaps in this view.
explore: The true-colour picture was built from six exposures taken through B, V and R filters with the Burrell Schmidt telescope, which belongs to Case Western Reserve University's Warner and Swasey Observatory and stands on Kitt Peak, near Tucson, Arizona. The images date from July 1995, during the Research Experiences for Undergraduates program run at Kitt Peak National Observatory with support from the National Science Foundation.

understand.summary: The Burrell Schmidt telescope on Kitt Peak photographed M23 in visible light through B, V and R filters, and the frames were combined into what NOIRLab describes as a true-colour picture.
understand.eye: Stacked telescope exposures collect far more light than the eye can, so many more faint stars appear here than anyone would see looking at the cluster directly.

scaleExtra: M23 is some 2200 light-years away and about 20 light-years across, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A dense field of stars with scattered black patches where dust hides distant stars, and a bright foreground star at upper right.

caption: The Sagittarius Star Cloud, M24, imaged by the Burrell Schmidt telescope at Kitt Peak
story: This picture covers most of the central part of M24, the Sagittarius Star Cloud. A small open star cluster, NGC 6603, sits toward the upper left, and two dark nebulae, Barnard 92 and Barnard 93, lie toward the upper right.

M24 is an unusual entry in Messier's original catalogue. He recorded it as a big patch of "nebulosity" about a degree and a half across, but it is not a single object. Instead it is a chance lineup on the sky: a great many stars lying at many different distances from us, one behind another, all belonging to the Sagittarius spiral arm of our own Galaxy.

The dark nebulae are a reminder that the space between stars is not empty. A dark nebula is a cloud of gas and dust dense enough to block the light of stars behind it, so it shows up as a shadow against a busier background of stars.
explore: The image is a mosaic. Seven frames were taken through B, V and R filters in June 1996 with Case Western Reserve University's Burrell Schmidt telescope, part of its Warner and Swasey Observatory, near Tucson, Arizona, on Kitt Peak, as part of the Research Experiences for Undergraduates program supported by the National Science Foundation. Another nine frames were added from the same telescope in September 1997.

understand.summary: The Burrell Schmidt telescope on Kitt Peak recorded this star field in visible light through B, V and R filters, and many frames were stitched into a mosaic; exactly how each filter was coloured is not published.
understand.eye: The mosaic's long exposures gather far more light than the eye, so the camera picks out a great many faint individual stars.

alt: A crowded field of stars from the Sagittarius Star Cloud, with a small star cluster at upper left and dark dusty patches at upper right.

caption: The open star cluster M21, imaged by the Burrell Schmidt telescope at Kitt Peak
story: This approximately true-colour view shows M21, also known as NGC 6531, an open star cluster in the constellation Sagittarius. Its stars are strongly concentrated toward the middle and span a wide range of brightness, even though the cluster probably has fewer than 60 members.

An open cluster is a loose family of stars that were born together from the same cloud of gas and dust. Over time such groups tend to drift apart. M21 is most likely quite young, which for a star cluster means only a few million years old. How far away it lies is still uncertain.

On the sky, M21 sits quite close to M20, the Trifid Nebula, as a lower-resolution, wider-field picture of the area shows. Clusters like M21 are useful to astronomers because their stars share a common origin, so differences between them reveal how stars of different masses develop.
explore: The picture combines eleven images taken through B, V and R filters in July 1995 and June 1996 with Case Western Reserve University's Burrell Schmidt telescope, part of its Warner and Swasey Observatory, on Kitt Peak, near Tucson, Arizona. They were made during the Research Experiences for Undergraduates program at Kitt Peak National Observatory. The field is 28.8 arcminutes across.

understand.summary: The Burrell Schmidt telescope on Kitt Peak captured M21 in visible light using B, V and R filters, combined into an approximately true-colour picture.
understand.eye: Because the camera gathered light over long exposures, it records many fainter stars than the eye could pick out, though the colours are meant to be close to natural.

alt: A compact group of stars of varied brightness, concentrated toward the centre of a starry field.

caption: The elliptical galaxy M105 and neighbours in the Leo I group, imaged by the KPNO 0.9-meter telescope
story: Three galaxies share this frame. M105 is the one on the right, a smooth elliptical galaxy classed as type E1. Above and to the left of centre is NGC 3384, another member of the same group, and at the bottom left sits a galaxy that lies far behind them in the background.

M105 is the brightest galaxy in the Leo I group, a gathering that also includes M95, M96 and a number of fainter galaxies. The whole group is about 40 million light-years away. Elliptical galaxies like M105 lack spiral arms and appear as soft, rounded glows of mostly older stars.

Its light fades so evenly from centre to edge that astronomers once used M105 as a standard for measuring how brightness is spread across galaxies. Closer study later showed that it is not quite as smooth, or as standard, as first thought, which the caption notes is the usual fate of any galaxy examined closely enough.
explore: This CCD colour composite was taken with the 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory on 5 February 1996 (Universal Time). Every picture of M105 includes NGC 3384, because the two sit so close together on the sky.

understand.summary: A CCD camera on the 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak recorded these galaxies in visible light, and the frames were combined into a colour composite; the colour mapping is not published.
understand.eye: The camera's exposures gather far more light than the eye, bringing out the extended glow of all three galaxies.

scaleExtra: The Leo I group is about 40 million light-years away, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A smooth, rounded galaxy at right, a second galaxy above and left of centre, and a smaller background galaxy at bottom left.
flags: caption names NGC 3379 both as M105 (title) and as the background galaxy at bottom left

caption: The spiral galaxy M99, imaged by the KPNO 0.9-meter telescope
story: We look straight down onto M99, a spiral galaxy of type Sc in the constellation Coma Berenices. Because it faces us, its spiral arms are on full display. The picture was processed, or "flattened", so that arm structure shows up both close to the nucleus and out toward the galaxy's faint edges.

Most images of M99 either let the bright centre overflow into a white blob or stop before the dim outskirts appear. Compressing the range of brightness this way keeps both ends visible in a single frame.

M99 belongs to the Virgo Cluster of galaxies, the dominant cluster in our Local Supercluster, roughly 60 million light-years away. It also has a place in history: in 1848 Lord Rosse recognised its spiral shape, making it only the second such nebula known. His first had been M51, three years earlier in 1845.
explore: The 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory took this picture in February 1996. The Virgo Cluster also contains many other Messier galaxies, among them M49, M58, M59, M60, M61 and M84, as well as M85, M86, M87, M88 and M89, plus M90, M91, M98 and M100.

understand.summary: The 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak captured M99 in visible light, and the image's brightness scale was compressed to show both core and outer arms; the colour mapping is not published.
understand.eye: A camera can record a far wider range of brightness than the eye picks out in a faint galaxy, and the processing here squeezes that range so the dim outer arms and bright centre can be seen together.

scaleExtra: The Virgo Cluster, which includes M99, is about 60 million light-years away, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A face-on spiral galaxy with clearly defined arms winding out from a bright centre.

caption: The star cluster M71 in Sagitta, imaged by the KPNO 0.9-meter telescope
story: This composite shows M71, also catalogued as NGC 6838, a star cluster in the small constellation Sagitta, the Arrow. The field shown is 9.1 arcminutes across.

M71 sits on a borderline. Most people would probably call it a globular cluster, even though it looks rather spread out, but some still argue it is simply an open cluster that happens to be concentrated toward its centre. The fact that the argument continues shows how fine the line between a loose globular cluster and a dense open cluster can be.

A globular cluster is a tightly packed, roughly spherical swarm of old stars, while an open cluster is a looser, usually younger group. M71 lies about 12000 light-years from us and is fairly small, probably only 30 or so light-years across. More stars lie farther out, but whether they really belong to the cluster is uncertain.
explore: The images behind this composite were taken in July 1998 with the 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory, during the Research Experiences for Undergraduates program run at the observatory with support from the National Science Foundation.

understand.summary: The 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak recorded M71 in visible light, and several images were combined into a colour composite; the filters and colour mapping are not published.
understand.eye: The telescope's exposures gather much more light than the eye, so the cluster's many faint stars are resolved individually rather than blurring into a hazy patch.

scaleExtra: M71 is about 12000 light-years away and probably around 30 light-years across, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A loose, rounded concentration of stars in a starry field.

caption: The globular cluster M5, imaged by the Burrell Schmidt telescope at Kitt Peak
story: This approximately true-colour picture shows M5, also known as NGC 5904, a globular cluster in the constellation Serpens. It is perhaps the finest globular cluster that can be seen from the northern hemisphere, and under excellent conditions it is even faintly visible without a telescope.

A globular cluster is a dense, ball-shaped swarm of stars held together by their shared gravity. M5 is an elongated example, and it ranks among the largest and oldest such clusters, with an age that may be about 13 billion years. Its stars formed very early, long before our Sun existed.

The cluster lies almost 25000 light-years from us. Its light has therefore been travelling for about as long as that number of years before reaching the telescope on Kitt Peak, so we see M5 as it was long before any human history was written.
explore: Fourteen images were combined to make this view, taken through B, V and R filters in June and July 1997 with Case Western Reserve University's Burrell Schmidt telescope, part of its Warner and Swasey Observatory, on Kitt Peak, near Tucson, Arizona. The work was part of the Research Experiences for Undergraduates program at Kitt Peak National Observatory. The field is 34.6 arcminutes across.

understand.summary: The Burrell Schmidt telescope on Kitt Peak captured M5 in visible light through B, V and R filters, and the images were combined into an approximately true-colour picture.
understand.eye: To the unaided eye, M5 is at best a faint fuzzy spot; the telescope's long exposures separate it into a great many individual stars.

scaleExtra: M5 lies almost 25000 light-years away, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A dense, elongated ball of stars in a field of scattered stars.

caption: The open star cluster M103, imaged by the Kitt Peak 2.1-meter telescope
story: This true-colour picture shows M103, also catalogued as NGC 581, a star cluster in the constellation Cassiopeia. The bright pair of stars at the upper right is a binary that does not belong to the cluster. The whole view is only 8.6 arcminutes across.

M103 is one of the more remote open clusters, at roughly 8000 light-years away. It looks fairly small on the sky, but at that distance its modest size still corresponds to a diameter of about 14 light-years. Its age is debated; it may be more than 20 million years old.

The cluster has an interesting place in the history of the Messier catalogue. It is one of the extra objects that were added based on observations by Méchain, and Messier himself never actually looked at it. An open cluster like this is a loose group of stars that formed together.
explore: The picture combines fifteen images taken through B, V and R filters with the 2.1-meter telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory. They were all captured on a single night, 24 December 2000, which the caption cheerfully notes was Christmas Eve.

understand.summary: The 2.1-meter telescope at Kitt Peak recorded M103 in visible light through B, V and R filters, and the frames were combined into a true-colour picture.
understand.eye: Long exposures on a large telescope gather much more light than the eye, so many faint stars appear alongside the brighter cluster members.

scaleExtra: M103 is about 8000 light-years away and about 14 light-years across, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A scattered group of stars, with a bright pair of stars at upper right.

caption: The globular cluster M92, imaged by the Burrell Schmidt telescope at Kitt Peak
story: This approximately true-colour picture shows M92, also catalogued as NGC 6341, a globular cluster in the constellation Hercules. Under excellent sky conditions it can even be seen with the naked eye.

A globular cluster is a tightly packed, roughly spherical collection of very old stars bound together by gravity. M92 lies about 28000 light-years away and measures more than 100 light-years across, which means an enormous number of stars are squeezed into the ball seen here.

M92 has a well-known neighbour on the sky, the globular cluster M13, also in Hercules. Compared with M13, M92 is slightly farther away and a little younger. Clusters like these are valuable to astronomers because all their stars formed at about the same time, making them natural laboratories for studying how stars age.
explore: The images for this picture were taken in June 1996 using B, V and R filters with Case Western Reserve University's Burrell Schmidt telescope, part of its Warner and Swasey Observatory, near Tucson, Arizona, on Kitt Peak, as part of the Research Experiences for Undergraduates program at Kitt Peak National Observatory. The field is 28.8 arcminutes across.

understand.summary: The Burrell Schmidt telescope on Kitt Peak recorded M92 in visible light through B, V and R filters, combined into an approximately true-colour picture.
understand.eye: To the naked eye M92 is at best a faint smudge; the telescope's exposures resolve it into many individual stars.

scaleExtra: M92 is about 28000 light-years away and more than 100 light-years across, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A dense, round ball of stars set in a field of scattered stars.
flags: caption gives an age of about 15 billion years, older than current estimates for the universe; omitted from story

caption: The spiral galaxy M90, imaged by the Kitt Peak 0.9-meter telescope
story: This CCD composite shows M90, also listed as NGC 4569, a large Sb-type spiral galaxy in the constellation Virgo. To its north lies a smaller spiral, IC 3583, which has a high surface brightness and is clearly visible in this picture.

IC 3583 appears somewhat distorted. That odd appearance led the astronomer H. C. Arp to include the pair in his Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies, a catalogue of galaxies with unusual shapes, many of them thought to be disturbed by neighbours.

Despite its size, M90 appears to have relatively little mass, which would make it a galaxy of low density. It belongs to the Virgo Cluster of galaxies, the dominant cluster in our Local Supercluster, at a distance of about 60 million light-years. A galaxy cluster is a large family of galaxies bound together by gravity.
explore: The composite was taken in April 1998 with the 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak. The Virgo Cluster also contains many other Messier galaxies, including M49, M58, M59, M60, M61 and M84, as well as M85, M86, M87, M88 and M89, plus M91, M98, M99 and M100.

understand.summary: A CCD camera on the Kitt Peak 0.9-meter telescope recorded M90 in visible light, and the images were combined into a composite; the colour mapping is not published.
understand.eye: The camera's exposures gather far more light than the eye, bringing out the extended disc of the galaxy and its smaller neighbour.

scaleExtra: The Virgo Cluster, to which M90 belongs, is about 60 million light-years away, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A large spiral galaxy with a smaller, bright galaxy nearby to the north.

caption: Arp 104, Keenan's System, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter telescope at Kitt Peak
story: Two spiral galaxies are joined here by a slender, blue bridge. This pair is Arp 104, also called Keenan's System: NGC 5216 is at the bottom and NGC 5218 at the top, in the constellation Ursa Major.

The thin stream linking them is made of gas, and new stars are forming inside it. It was produced when the two galaxies swept past one another and their mutual gravity pulled gas out of them. The newborn stars in the stream are hot and massive, and their light is what gives it a blue colour.

The stream stretches for about 150,000 light-years. Encounters like this one show that galaxies are not isolated islands: a close pass can reshape them, drag material across intergalactic space and set off fresh bursts of star formation far from either galaxy's centre.
explore: The picture comes from the wide-field Mosaic camera of Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. It is oriented with north at the top and east to the left.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter telescope observed Arp 104 through B, V and I filters, shown as blue, green and red respectively; B and V are visible light and I lies at the red edge of the visible, reaching into the near-infrared.
understand.eye: The faint gas stream is far too dim to see by eye; the camera's long exposures and the I filter, which extends toward light the eye barely senses, bring it out.

scaleExtra: The gas stream joining the two galaxies is about 150,000 light-years long, according to NOIRLab.
alt: Two spiral galaxies, one above the other, connected by a thin blue stream of gas.

caption: The spiral galaxy M94, imaged by the KPNO 0.9-meter telescope
story: At the heart of M94 is an extremely bright inner region. Around it runs a blue ring made of young star clusters; next comes a dimmer yellowish zone of older stars edged with traces of young stars, and farther out still, a much fainter outer ring. This is the spiral galaxy M94, of type Sab, in the constellation Canes Venatici.

Seeing all these layers in one picture takes special handling. The brightness scale was drastically compressed, so that the glaring centre and the very dim outer ring can both be shown without one swamping the other.

That same stretch also brings out quite a few small, faint galaxies scattered in the background, far beyond M94. Some astronomers place M94 in a group with M64 and several fainter galaxies, while others do not, so its family ties remain a matter of debate.
explore: The picture was taken in May 1998 with the 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory. The field is 17.0 arcminutes across.

understand.summary: The 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak captured M94 in visible light, and the image's brightness range was heavily compressed to show every ring at once; the colour mapping is not published.
understand.eye: A camera can record a much wider range of brightness than can be shown directly, so compressing the scale reveals the faint outer ring that would otherwise be lost next to the bright core.

alt: A spiral galaxy with a very bright centre, a blue ring, a yellowish zone and a faint outer ring, with small faint galaxies in the background.

caption: The open clusters M35 and NGC 2158, imaged by the Burrell Schmidt telescope at Kitt Peak
story: Two star clusters share this approximately true-colour view. The large, scattered one is M35, an open cluster in the constellation Gemini. Toward the lower right, to the south-west, sits NGC 2158, a fainter but more compact neighbour.

M35 holds a couple of hundred stars and lies about 2800 light-years away. At an age of some 110 million years it is a youthful group by stellar standards. Under good conditions it can be seen with the naked eye, while NGC 2158 is much harder to pick out through small telescopes.

Here, though, the smaller cluster stands out clearly. The caption credits this to the camera on a research telescope at a good mountain site, which can record faint, closely packed stars that a backyard instrument struggles to separate. An open cluster is a loose family of stars that formed together from one cloud of gas.
explore: Twelve images went into this picture, taken through B, V and R filters in January 1997 with Case Western Reserve University's Burrell Schmidt telescope, part of its Warner and Swasey Observatory on Kitt Peak, near Tucson, Arizona.

understand.summary: The Burrell Schmidt telescope on Kitt Peak recorded this field in visible light with a CCD camera through B, V and R filters, combined into an approximately true-colour picture.
understand.eye: The camera collects far more light than the eye, so the compact NGC 2158, hard to see in small telescopes, shows up clearly here.

scaleExtra: M35 is about 2800 light-years away, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A broad scattering of bright stars, with a smaller, denser cluster of faint stars toward the lower right.

caption: The open star cluster M41, imaged by the Burrell Schmidt telescope at Kitt Peak
story: Among the many stars in this approximately true-colour picture, a few glow orange. These are red giants belonging to M41, an open cluster in the constellation Canis Major; red giants like these always look orange in images such as this one. The bright star in the lower left corner, the south-east, is a blue giant in the foreground and not part of the cluster.
M41 is a modest group of only about one hundred stars. It lies roughly 2300 light-years away and spans around 25 light-years, and it is about 200 million years old.

A red giant is a star that has used up the hydrogen fuel in its core and swelled up, its cooler outer layers giving it a warmer colour. Finding several of them here tells astronomers that the cluster's heaviest stars have already begun to reach this late stage of their lives.
explore: The picture was assembled from eleven images taken through B, V and R filters in September 1997 with Case Western Reserve University's Burrell Schmidt telescope at its Warner and Swasey Observatory on Kitt Peak, near Tucson, Arizona. The field measures 42.3 arcminutes across.

understand.summary: The Burrell Schmidt telescope on Kitt Peak captured M41 in visible light through B, V and R filters, combined into an approximately true-colour picture.
understand.eye: Star colours are hard for the eye to perceive in dim light, but the camera records them, so the orange giants and the blue foreground star stand out.

scaleExtra: M41 is roughly 2300 light-years away and around 25 light-years across, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A scattered cluster of stars including several orange ones, with a bright star in the lower left corner.

caption: The globular cluster M54, imaged by the KPNO 0.9-meter telescope
story: This composite shows M54, also catalogued as NGC 6715, a globular cluster in Sagittarius. It appears bright but small on the sky, and its crowded core is too dense to be split into separate stars in this picture.

A globular cluster is a tightly packed ball of old stars, held together by their combined gravity. Most globular clusters orbit our own Milky Way, and for a long time M54 was assumed to be one of them, at a distance of some 60000 light-years.

There is now a claim that M54 actually belongs to another galaxy altogether: the Sagittarius Dwarf, a small member of the Local Group, the collection of galaxies that includes the Milky Way. If so, M54 would lie nearly 90000 light-years away, making it a visitor from outside our Galaxy that only appears to sit among Sagittarius's stars.
explore: The images for this composite were taken in July 1998 with the 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory, as part of the Research Experiences for Undergraduates program there, supported by the National Science Foundation. The field is 11.6 arcminutes across.

understand.summary: The 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak recorded M54 in visible light, and the images were combined into a composite; the filters and colour mapping are not published.
understand.eye: The telescope's exposures separate the cluster's outer stars, though even this camera cannot resolve the densely packed core.

scaleExtra: M54 was long thought to be about 60000 light-years away, though if it belongs to the Sagittarius Dwarf it would be nearly 90000 light-years away, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A small, bright ball of stars with an unresolved central glow.

caption: The open star cluster M34, imaged by the Burrell Schmidt telescope at Kitt Peak
story: This approximately true-colour picture shows M34, also listed as NGC 1039, an open star cluster that lies in the direction of the constellation Perseus. Under good conditions it can be seen with the naked eye.
M34 lies some 1400 light-years away. About a hundred stars make it up, spread through a region roughly a dozen light-years across.

An open cluster is a loose group of stars that formed together from the same cloud of gas and dust. Because they share an origin, the stars have similar ages and chemical makeup, which makes such clusters useful for comparing how stars of different masses evolve. Over long stretches of time, the gravity of the rest of the Galaxy tends to pull open clusters apart, so their members gradually drift off to join the general population of stars. Compared with the dense globular clusters, open clusters are usually younger and much more loosely bound.
explore: The images were taken through B, V and R filters in July 1996 with Case Western Reserve University's Burrell Schmidt telescope, at its Warner and Swasey Observatory near Tucson, Arizona, on Kitt Peak, as part of the Research Experiences for Undergraduates program at Kitt Peak National Observatory. The field is 34.6 arcminutes across.

understand.summary: The Burrell Schmidt telescope on Kitt Peak recorded M34 in visible light through B, V and R filters, combined into an approximately true-colour picture.
understand.eye: To the naked eye M34 is a faint hazy patch; the telescope's exposures show its individual stars and their colours.

scaleExtra: M34 is about 1400 light-years away and some dozen light-years across, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A loose scattering of bright stars against a field of fainter stars.

caption: The spiral galaxy M100, imaged by the WIYN 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak
story: Strong blue spiral arms, lit by young stars, wind around the centre of M100, a nearly face-on spiral galaxy of type Sc. Two small dwarf galaxies nearby also appear in the frame, and the picture manages to show them without letting M100's bright inner regions overflow into a white glare.

M100 ranks among the brighter members of the Virgo Cluster, even though on the sky it lies within the neighbouring constellation Coma Berenices. A galaxy cluster is a large family of galaxies bound by gravity, and the Virgo Cluster is home to many of the galaxies in Messier's catalogue.
The blue colour of the arms is a sign of recent star birth. Young, hot, massive stars shine blue, and in a spiral galaxy they tend to be strung along the arms, where gas gathers and new stars form.
explore: The WIYN 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory captured this image on the night of 20 December 2002 (Universal Time), and covers 15.3 arcminutes. Other Messier galaxies in the Virgo Cluster include M49, M58, M59, M60, M61 and M84, as well as M85, M86, M87, M88 and M89, plus M90, M91, M98 and M99.

understand.summary: The WIYN 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak captured M100 in visible light; the filters and colour mapping are not published.
understand.eye: The camera's exposures gather far more light than the eye and can hold both the bright core and the fainter arms in one frame.

alt: A nearly face-on spiral galaxy with blue arms around a bright centre, and two small dwarf galaxies nearby.

caption: The Double Cluster, h and chi Persei, imaged by the Burrell Schmidt telescope at Kitt Peak
story: Two star clusters sit side by side in this colour picture. On the left is chi Persei, also called NGC 884, and beside it is h Persei, or NGC 869. Together they form the Double Cluster in the constellation Perseus, usually known by these transliterated Greek labels.

The pair lies about 7000 light-years from us, and the two clusters are less than 100 light-years apart. Open clusters, loose groups of stars born together, are quite common, but this pair is exceptional.

What sets it apart is how many young, bright O and B stars each cluster holds. These are the hottest and most massive kinds of stars, which burn through their fuel quickly and so do not last long; seeing so many of them marks both clusters as young. The two are also unusual for being so close together while still clearly separate.
explore: CCD images from September 1997 were used to make the picture with Case Western Reserve University's Burrell Schmidt telescope, part of its Warner and Swasey Observatory, on Kitt Peak in southwestern Arizona.

understand.summary: A CCD camera on the Burrell Schmidt telescope at Kitt Peak recorded the Double Cluster in visible light, combined into a colour picture; the colour mapping is not published.
understand.eye: The camera's exposures gather far more light than the eye, revealing many more faint stars and recording their colours.

scaleExtra: The two clusters are about 7000 light-years away and less than 100 light-years apart, according to NOIRLab.
alt: Two rich clusters of bright stars side by side in a dense star field.

caption: The globular cluster M10, imaged by the Burrell Schmidt telescope at Kitt Peak
story: This picture shows M10, also catalogued as NGC 6254, a globular cluster in the constellation Ophiuchus. It lies close on the sky to another globular cluster, M12, and shines at seventh magnitude.
M10 measures about 70 light-years across and lies about 16000 light-years away. On the sky it spans roughly half the width of the full Moon.

A globular cluster is a dense, ball-shaped swarm of very old stars bound together by their shared gravity. The stars are packed most tightly toward the centre and thin out toward the edges. Clusters like this orbit around the centre of our Galaxy, often far above or below its disc, and because their stars all formed at about the same time, they serve as useful records of the Galaxy's early history.
explore: The picture was made from CCD images taken in June 1996 with Case Western Reserve University's Burrell Schmidt telescope, part of its Warner and Swasey Observatory, on Kitt Peak in southwestern Arizona, during the Research Experiences for Undergraduates program at Kitt Peak National Observatory.

understand.summary: A CCD camera on the Burrell Schmidt telescope at Kitt Peak recorded M10 in visible light; the filters and colour mapping are not published.
understand.eye: The camera's exposures gather far more light than the eye, resolving many of the cluster's individual stars.

scaleExtra: M10 is about 16000 light-years away and about 70 light-years across, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A round, densely packed cluster of stars that thins toward its edges.

caption: The Beehive Cluster, M44, imaged by the Burrell Schmidt telescope at Kitt Peak
story: This approximately true-colour picture shows M44, the Beehive Cluster, also called Praesepe, which is Latin for manger. It is an open cluster in the constellation Cancer, and one of the nearest open clusters to us, close to 600 light-years away.
The Beehive is easy to see with the naked eye and covers a patch of sky more than twice as wide as the full Moon. Because it is so obvious, people have noticed it since prehistoric times.

It also has a place in the history of the telescope. When Galileo acquired his new instrument, the Beehive was among the first things he pointed it at. An open cluster like this is a loose group of stars that formed together, and being so close makes M44 a convenient place to study how such stars develop.
explore: Fifteen images went into this picture, taken through B, V and R filters in January 1997 with Case Western Reserve University's Burrell Schmidt telescope at its Warner and Swasey Observatory, on Kitt Peak near Tucson, Arizona.

understand.summary: The Burrell Schmidt telescope on Kitt Peak captured the Beehive in visible light through B, V and R filters, combined into an approximately true-colour picture.
understand.eye: The Beehive is easy to see with the naked eye, but the camera separates it into individual stars and records their colours.

scaleExtra: The Beehive is close to 600 light-years away, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A wide, loose group of bright stars spread across a starry field.

caption: The globular cluster M55, imaged by the Burrell Schmidt telescope at Kitt Peak
story: This composite shows M55, also catalogued as NGC 6809, a globular cluster in the constellation Sagittarius. It is fairly large on the sky, spanning about two thirds of the Moon's diameter, but its stars are spread very loosely, giving it an appearance that is barely like a globular cluster at all.
M55 lies about 18000 light-years away and is about 100 light-years across.

A globular cluster is typically a dense, ball-shaped swarm of old stars, packed so tightly toward the centre that the core often blurs into a single glow. Clusters vary in how concentrated they are, and loose ones like M55 let telescopes pick out individual stars even near the middle. Because all of a cluster's stars formed at roughly the same time, comparing them helps astronomers work out how stars of different masses age, and globular clusters in particular preserve a record of our Galaxy's distant past.
explore: The images for this composite were taken in June 1996 with Case Western Reserve University's Burrell Schmidt telescope at its Warner and Swasey Observatory, as part of the Research Experiences for Undergraduates program at Kitt Peak National Observatory, supported by the National Science Foundation.

understand.summary: The Burrell Schmidt telescope on Kitt Peak recorded M55 in visible light, combined into a composite; the filters and colour mapping are not published.
understand.eye: The camera's exposures gather much more light than the eye, resolving many stars across the cluster's loose spread.

scaleExtra: M55 is about 18000 light-years away and about 100 light-years across, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A large, loosely packed cluster of stars in a starry field.

caption: The open star cluster M50, imaged by the Burrell Schmidt telescope at Kitt Peak
story: This approximately true-colour picture shows M50, also listed as NGC 2323, an open cluster in the constellation Monoceros, the Unicorn. It is a cluster of modest size, holding perhaps a couple of hundred stars. Some observers with more imaginative eyes have described its shape as a heart.
M50 lies about 3000 light-years away and measures around 20 light-years across.

An open cluster is a loose group of stars that were born together from the same cloud of gas and dust. Because its members share a birthplace and an age, a cluster is a natural experiment: stars of different masses start out together, and the differences between them show how mass shapes the way a star lives. Open clusters are only loosely bound, so over time the pull of the rest of the Galaxy tends to scatter their members, and the stars eventually drift away to mix with the general population.
explore: Twelve images went into this picture, taken through B, V and R filters in September 1997 with Case Western Reserve University's Burrell Schmidt telescope, at its Warner and Swasey Observatory on Kitt Peak near Tucson, Arizona.

understand.summary: The Burrell Schmidt telescope on Kitt Peak captured M50 in visible light through B, V and R filters, combined into an approximately true-colour picture.
understand.eye: The camera's exposures gather far more light than the eye and record star colours that are hard to see in dim light.

scaleExtra: M50 is about 3000 light-years away and around 20 light-years across, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A modest cluster of stars scattered across a starry field.

caption: The spiral galaxy M58, imaged by the Kitt Peak 0.9-meter telescope
story: This CCD composite shows M58, also catalogued as NGC 4579, a spiral galaxy in the constellation Virgo. It is classed as type SBc, a barred spiral, although its bar is not prominent, and some astronomers have placed it somewhere between normal and barred spirals.

In a barred spiral, a straight band of stars runs across the centre, and the spiral arms begin from the ends of that bar rather than from the core itself. How strong the bar is varies from galaxy to galaxy, which is why borderline cases like M58 can be classified in more than one way.

M58 belongs to the Virgo Cluster of galaxies, the dominant cluster in our Local Supercluster. The cluster is about 60 million light-years away. A galaxy cluster is a large family of galaxies bound together by gravity, and Virgo holds many galaxies bright enough to appear in Messier's catalogue.
explore: The composite was taken in April 1998 with the 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak. Other Messier galaxies in the Virgo Cluster include M49, M59, M60, M61 and M84, as well as M85, M86, M87, M88 and M89, plus M90, M91, M98, M99 and M100.

understand.summary: A CCD camera on the Kitt Peak 0.9-meter telescope recorded M58 in visible light, and the images were combined into a composite; the colour mapping is not published.
understand.eye: The camera's exposures gather far more light than the eye, showing structure in the galaxy that would be hard to see directly.

scaleExtra: The Virgo Cluster, which includes M58, is about 60 million light-years away, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A spiral galaxy with a weak central bar.

caption: The open star cluster M37, imaged by the KPNO 0.9-meter telescope
story: This colour composite shows M37, also listed as NGC 2099, an open star cluster in the constellation Auriga. The field shown is 14.2 by 11.3 arcminutes.

M37 contains approximately 200 stars within a diameter of 27 light-years, and it lies some 4600 light-years from us. It shares its part of the sky with two other clusters, M36 and M38, and of the three it is the brightest and the richest.

An open cluster is a loose group of stars that formed together from one cloud of gas and dust, so its members share roughly the same age and makeup. That makes clusters like M37 useful for studying how stars change over time: the heavier stars age faster than the lighter ones, so comparing them within one cluster shows different stages of stellar life side by side. Such clusters are only loosely held together, and over time their stars slowly drift apart.
explore: The picture was made from CCD images taken in December 1994 with the 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory, near Tucson, Arizona.

understand.summary: A CCD camera on the 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak recorded M37 in visible light, and the images were combined into a colour composite; the colour mapping is not published.
understand.eye: The camera's exposures gather far more light than the eye, so many of the cluster's fainter stars appear that a small telescope would not show.

scaleExtra: M37 is some 4600 light-years away and 27 light-years across, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A rich open cluster of stars.

caption: The open star cluster M36, imaged by the KPNO 0.9-meter telescope
story: This colour composite shows M36, also catalogued as NGC 1960, an open star cluster in the southern part of the constellation Auriga. The field shown is 20.4 arcminutes across.

M36 is one of three bright open clusters in that region of the sky, alongside M37 and M38. The three sit at similar distances, about 4000 light-years from us. What sets M36 apart is its youth: it is significantly younger than its two neighbours and contains no evolved red giant stars.

That missing ingredient is a clue to its age. When a star exhausts the hydrogen in its core it swells into a red giant, and the most massive stars reach that stage first. In an older cluster, some members have already made the change. In M36 none has yet, which fits a cluster that has not been around long. An open cluster like this is a loose family of stars born together from the same cloud of gas.
explore: The composite was made from CCD images taken in January 1997 with the 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory, near Tucson, Arizona.

understand.summary: A CCD camera on the 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak recorded M36 in visible light, and the images were combined into a colour composite; the colour mapping is not published.
understand.eye: The camera's exposures show many more faint stars than the eye could see, and record colours that are hard to perceive in dim light.

scaleExtra: M36 and its neighbours M37 and M38 all lie about 4000 light-years away, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A loose cluster of bright stars scattered across a starry field.

caption: The globular cluster M75, imaged by the KPNO 0.9-meter telescope
story: This image shows M75, also catalogued as NGC 6864, a globular cluster in Sagittarius. It is quite centrally condensed, with its stars crowding strongly toward the middle.

M75 is one of the more distant globular clusters. It lies more than 61000 light-years away, and some sources put it as far as 100000 light-years. It is also big and brilliant, spanning more than 100 light-years and shining a couple of hundred thousand times more brightly than the Sun.

A globular cluster is a dense, roughly spherical swarm of old stars held together by gravity. Many such clusters orbit our Galaxy, some far out in its outskirts, and their stars are among the oldest known. Because all the stars in one cluster formed at about the same time, globular clusters help astronomers trace the early history of the Milky Way and test ideas about how stars age.
explore: The image was built from data gathered in October 1998 with the 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory. The field is 9.1 arcminutes across.

understand.summary: The 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak recorded M75 in visible light; the filters and colour mapping are not published.
understand.eye: The camera's exposures gather far more light than the eye, showing the concentrated glow of the cluster's stars.

scaleExtra: M75 is more than 61000 light-years away, possibly as much as 100000, and over 100 light-years across, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A compact, bright ball of stars that is densest at its centre.

caption: Star trails over Maunakea, Hawaiʻi
story: Stars sweep across the sky as trails above Maunakea in Hawaiʻi in this classic star-trail photograph. The landscape below is lit by a first-quarter Moon, which stayed up for the whole time the pictures were being taken.

The trails were not captured in a single shot. More than 150 separate digital photographs, each lasting one minute, were stacked together in Photoshop, following a technique described in the March 2004 issue of Sky and Telescope magazine.

Stacking works because each short frame records the stars as small dots or short dashes in slightly different places. Layered together, those positions join up into continuous arcs. The arcs themselves come from Earth's rotation: as our planet turns, the whole sky appears to wheel slowly overhead, and a camera that stays fixed to the ground records that apparent motion as a streak of light for every star bright enough to register.
explore: The same set of images was also used to make a high-definition time-lapse movie, in which the individual frames are played in sequence so the sky can be seen turning.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph made with a digital camera: over 150 one-minute exposures in visible light were stacked in Photoshop to build the trails.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as fixed points at any moment; only by adding many exposures together does a photograph reveal their slow apparent motion as trails.

alt: Star trails across the night sky above a moonlit landscape on Maunakea.

caption: The spiral galaxy M65, imaged by the WIYN 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak
story: This image shows M65, also catalogued as NGC 3623, an Sa-type spiral galaxy in the constellation Leo. The field shown is 7.9 by 11.9 arcminutes.
M65 lies at a distance of about 35 million light-years. It appears to form a trio with two neighbours, the galaxies M66 and NGC 3628, which share its part of the sky.

Spiral galaxies are sorted into types by the size of their central bulge and how tightly their arms are wound. Type Sa galaxies sit at one end of that range, with a relatively large, bright bulge and smooth, tightly wrapped arms. Galaxies grouped together like M65 and its companions are bound by gravity, and over long spans of time their mutual pull can tug on one another's shapes and stir up gas. Small groups such as this are common, and our own Milky Way belongs to one too.
explore: The WIYN 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory recorded it on the night of 19 December 2002 (Universal Time).

understand.summary: The WIYN 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak recorded M65 in visible light; the filters and colour mapping are not published.
understand.eye: Through a small telescope M65 is a faint elongated smudge; the camera's exposures gather enough light to show the galaxy's structure.

scaleExtra: M65 is about 35 million light-years away, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A spiral galaxy seen at an angle, with a bright central bulge.

caption: Star trails and a laser beam over Gemini South, Cerro Pachón
story: Stars trace trails across the sky in this photograph taken from the summit of Cerro Pachón, while the laser guide star system of the Gemini South telescope is in action. Gemini South is part of the International Gemini Observatory, which NSF NOIRLab runs as one of its programs.

The laser is a tool for sharpening the telescope's view. Its light interacts with particles high in Earth's upper atmosphere, creating a point of reference in the sky. By watching that artificial reference, the system can correct the telescope's optics in real time to compensate for turbulence in the air.

Turbulence is the reason stars twinkle. Pockets of air at different temperatures bend starlight in constantly shifting ways, blurring the images that even large telescopes collect. Correcting for this in real time is called adaptive optics, and a laser guide star lets it work in any part of the sky, not only near a bright natural star.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken with a camera at Cerro Pachón in visible light; the camera settings and processing are not published.
understand.eye: A long exposure lets the stars drift into trails as Earth turns, whereas the eye sees stars as points.

alt: Star trails over the summit of Cerro Pachón, with the Gemini South laser guide star system in action.

caption: The globular cluster M28, imaged by the KPNO 0.9-meter telescope
story: This image shows M28, also catalogued as NGC 6626, a globular cluster in the constellation Sagittarius. It has been stretched to reveal its inner regions, which are usually saturated, or burned out to pure white, in most pictures of the cluster.
M28 is slightly elliptical in shape rather than perfectly round. It measures around 80 light-years across and lies some 18000 light-years from us.

A globular cluster is a dense, ball-shaped swarm of old stars bound together by their shared gravity. The stars crowd most tightly toward the centre, which is why the middle of a cluster is so bright that a camera often cannot record any detail there. Stretching an image compresses its range of brightness, so both the crowded core and the thinner edges can be shown in one view. Because their stars formed together long ago, globular clusters give astronomers a record of our Galaxy's early history.
explore: The image was created from data taken in November 1998 with the 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory. The field is 8.5 arcminutes across.

understand.summary: The 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak recorded M28 in visible light, and the image was stretched to show the crowded core; the filters and colour mapping are not published.
understand.eye: A camera can capture a wider range of brightness than can be shown directly; stretching the image lets the dense centre appear without being swamped.

scaleExtra: M28 is around 80 light-years across and some 18000 light-years away, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A slightly oval ball of stars with detail visible in its crowded centre.

caption: The globular cluster M14, imaged by the KPNO 0.9-meter telescope
story: This picture shows M14, also catalogued as NGC 6402, a globular cluster in the constellation Ophiuchus. Compared with many globular clusters it is somewhat loose, and it is very nearly circular on the sky, with only a very small ellipticity.
Ellipticity is simply a measure of how far an object's outline departs from a perfect circle. M14 lies about 29000 light-years away and is about 72 light-years across.

A globular cluster is a dense, roughly spherical collection of old stars held together by gravity. Clusters differ in how tightly their stars are packed, and looser ones like M14 let a telescope pick out individual stars farther toward the centre. These clusters orbit our Galaxy and contain some of its oldest stars, so they are valuable for studying how the Milky Way formed and how stars grow old.
explore: The picture was made from CCD images taken in April 1998 with the 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory. The field is 11.6 arcminutes across.

understand.summary: A CCD camera on the 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak recorded M14 in visible light; the filters and colour mapping are not published.
understand.eye: The camera's exposures gather far more light than the eye and resolve many of the cluster's individual stars.

scaleExtra: M14 is about 29000 light-years away and about 72 light-years across, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A round, somewhat loose ball of stars in a starry field.

caption: The starburst galaxy NGC 1313, imaged by the Gemini South telescope
story: Colourful clouds of gas blaze along the spiral arms of NGC 1313 in this view from the Gemini South 8-meter telescope in Chile. Those glowing clouds are a clear sign that the galaxy is forming stars at a furious pace.

NGC 1313 is a starburst galaxy, producing stars on a scale rarely seen in a galaxy of its size. It is a late-type barred spiral, about 15 million light-years away, and a relatively close neighbour of the Milky Way. Its shape is deformed, and its past is something of a mystery.

Starbursts are usually set off by a close encounter with another galaxy, yet NGC 1313 seems to be a lone drifter, far from any group. Astronomers have several ideas. Perhaps a thousand supernovae went off within a few million years, blowing a superbubble whose expansion triggered new stars. Perhaps an unseen companion punched through the disc, sending out shock waves like ripples in a pond. Or gas clouds may be falling into, or orbiting, the galaxy.
explore: No single explanation has won out, so the combination of NGC 1313's distorted shape and its high rate of star formation remains an open puzzle. The image was made with the GMOS-S instrument on Gemini South.

understand.summary: Gemini South's GMOS-S instrument imaged NGC 1313 in visible light through narrow filters that isolate glowing helium (He II), oxygen (O III) and hydrogen-alpha; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: Narrowband filters pick out the specific colours emitted by glowing gas, emphasising the star-forming clouds.

alt: A barred spiral galaxy with many colourful glowing gas clouds scattered along its arms.
flags: packet distance field says 14 million light-years; caption says some 15 million

caption: The Southern Pinwheel Galaxy, Messier 83, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope
story: We see Messier 83 face-on, its spiral arms lined with dark lanes of dust and dotted with reddish clouds of hydrogen gas where stars are forming. Around the edges of the frame, many background galaxies appear, all far more distant than the spiral itself.

Nicknamed the Southern Pinwheel, and also catalogued as NGC 5236, Messier 83 lies in the southern constellation Hydra, about 15 million light-years away. This is one of the deepest images ever made of it, combining more than 11 hours of exposure time.

That long exposure is what helps faint features appear, such as the far-off galaxies scattered behind it. The reddish clouds glow because young, hot stars inside them energise the surrounding hydrogen, making these patches markers of fresh star birth.
explore: The view was captured with the Dark Energy Camera, or DECam, a camera the US Department of Energy built. It is mounted on Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory's Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope, a Program of NSF NOIRLab.

understand.summary: DECam on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope observed M83 through u, g, r, i and z filters plus a hydrogen-alpha filter, spanning near-ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: More than 11 hours of combined exposure gathers vastly more light than the eye ever could, and the z filter reaches into near-infrared light that the eye cannot see.

alt: A face-on spiral galaxy with dark dust lanes and reddish patches along its arms, surrounded by small distant galaxies.

caption: The galaxy Centaurus A, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope
story: A luminous glow of stars surrounds dark tendrils of dust that hide the bright centre of Centaurus A. Red clouds of hydrogen and, at each end of that dark lane, large numbers of faint blue stars show where new stars are being born.

Seen toward the southern constellation Centaurus, the Centaur, Centaurus A lies more than 12 million light-years away. Its dust is left over from a collision in the past, when a giant elliptical galaxy absorbed a smaller spiral.

The merger did more than add dust. Along with large amounts of gas, the dust lane now hosts star formation across wide areas, and the red hydrogen clouds and many faint blue stars are the evidence. Collisions like this are a reminder that galaxies grow and change by swallowing one another, and that such events can spark fresh generations of stars.
explore: The image was taken with the Dark Energy Camera mounted on the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope. NOIRLab invites viewers to zoom into the image to see more.

understand.summary: DECam on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope observed Centaurus A through u, g, r, i and z filters plus a hydrogen-alpha filter, covering near-ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: The z filter records near-infrared light the eye cannot see, and the camera's long exposures bring out faint blue stars that would be invisible by eye.

scaleExtra: Centaurus A lies more than 12 million light-years away, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A glowing galaxy crossed by dark lanes of dust, with red clouds of hydrogen and faint blue stars at each end of the dust lane.

caption: Barnard's Galaxy, NGC 6822, imaged by the Blanco 4-meter Telescope
story: Glowing red regions are scattered throughout this dwarf galaxy, each one a site where stars are being born. Among them sit a number of enormous bubbles. This is Barnard's Galaxy, also catalogued as NGC 6822, a small neighbour of our Milky Way.

The red patches show that star birth is widespread across the galaxy despite its small size. Several of its regions are famous in their own right, studied ever since Edwin Hubble first detected them in 1925.

A dwarf galaxy is a small galaxy with far fewer stars than a large spiral like the Milky Way. Nearby examples like this one are valuable because they are close enough to be studied in detail, letting astronomers compare how stars form in a small system with how they form in our own.
explore: The image comes from Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory's Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope, operated by NSF NOIRLab, using the Mosaic II camera. NOIRLab describes it as its best view yet of this neighbouring galaxy.

understand.summary: The Mosaic II camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope observed Barnard's Galaxy through U, B, V, R and I filters plus narrow oxygen (O III) and hydrogen-alpha filters, covering near-ultraviolet to the edge of near-infrared light; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: Narrow filters isolate the light of glowing hydrogen and oxygen, emphasising star-forming regions and bubbles far too faint for the eye to see.

alt: A dwarf galaxy made of many stars, with glowing red star-forming regions and large bubbles scattered through it.

caption: The spiral galaxy Messier 106, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope at Kitt Peak
story: This view captures the whole of Messier 106, also known as NGC 4258: glowing spiral arms, dust lanes and wisps of gas near its centre, and slowly twisting bands of stars around its outer edges. Two dwarf galaxies also appear, UGC 7358 at the lower left and NGC 4248 at the lower right.
Messier 106 lies in the constellation Canes Venatici and is a popular target for amateur astronomers, since it can be spotted with a small telescope.

A spiral galaxy is a flat, rotating disc of stars, gas and dust, with arms that wind out from a bright central region. The arms glow because they hold concentrations of gas and young stars, while dust lanes block light from behind. Dwarf galaxies like the two nearby here are much smaller systems, and they are often found keeping company with larger galaxies.
explore: The image was taken with Kitt Peak National Observatory's Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope, part of NSF NOIRLab, using the Mosaic I camera.

understand.summary: The Mosaic I camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope observed Messier 106 through U, B and R filters plus a hydrogen-alpha filter, spanning near-ultraviolet and visible light; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: The large telescope's long exposures gather far more light than the eye, revealing the galaxy's faint outer bands and the dwarf galaxies nearby.

alt: A large spiral galaxy with glowing arms and central dust lanes, with two small dwarf galaxies at lower right and lower left.

caption: The starburst galaxy NGC 4449, imaged by the Gemini North telescope
story: Bright pinks and blues burst across this view of NGC 4449, scattered through the galaxy like confetti. Gemini North, which makes up half of the International Gemini Observatory, took the image, which was released to mark the telescope's 25th anniversary.

NGC 4449 is a textbook case of a starburst galaxy, a galaxy forming new stars far faster than usual. Here the burst is driven by galaxies interacting and mingling, as NGC 4449 slowly absorbs its smaller neighbours. It lies about 12 million light-years away, in the constellation Canes Venatici.

When galaxies interact, their gravity stirs and compresses clouds of gas, and dense gas is where stars are born. Encounters like the ones NGC 4449 is going through can therefore set off star birth across a whole galaxy, which is what makes it such a clear example of a starburst.
explore: The image was obtained by NOIRLab's Communication, Education and Engagement team for NOIRLab's Legacy Imaging Program, using the GMOS-N instrument on Gemini North.

understand.summary: Gemini North's GMOS-N instrument observed NGC 4449 in visible light through an r filter and narrow hydrogen-alpha and sulphur (S II) filters; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: Narrowband filters isolate the specific colours given off by glowing gas, so star-forming clouds stand out far more than they would to the eye through a telescope.

alt: A galaxy scattered with bright pink and blue patches of glowing gas and stars.

caption: The spiral galaxy M74, imaged by the Gemini North telescope
story: This colour picture shows NGC 628, better known as M74, a spiral galaxy in the constellation Pisces, nicknamed the Perfect Spiral in its release title. It was taken on Mauna Kea, Hawaiʻi, with the 8.1-meter Gemini North telescope, using an instrument that had just been commissioned: the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph, or GMOS.

To make the colour image, three separate pictures were combined as the red, green and blue layers of a composite. The observations were made on 13 and 14 August 2001, and the field covers 5.7 by 5.4 arcminutes.

A spiral galaxy is a flat, rotating disc of stars, gas and dust whose arms wind out from a bright central region. The arms stand out because they are where gas collects and young stars form. Galaxies like M74, seen with their arms laid out clearly, are useful for studying how that spiral pattern is organised.
explore: Although GMOS is a spectrograph, able to split light from many objects into spectra at once, it can also take direct images, as it did here during its commissioning, the period when a new instrument is tested on the telescope.

understand.summary: GMOS on Gemini North imaged M74 in visible and near-infrared light through g, r and i filters, combined into a red, green and blue composite; which filter went to which colour is not stated.
understand.eye: The i filter reaches into near-infrared light the eye cannot see, and an 8-meter mirror gathers far more light than a human eye.

alt: The spiral galaxy M74, shown in a colour composite.

caption: The irregular starburst galaxy IC 10, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope at Kitt Peak
story: This portrait from NOIRLab's Kitt Peak National Observatory shows IC 10, a disorderly irregular galaxy that is forming stars at a high rate. Besides many bright young stars, it hosts exotic Wolf-Rayet stars and a black hole.

Seen toward the constellation Cassiopeia, IC 10 is around 2 million light-years from Earth. That sounds enormously far, yet it places the galaxy within our Local Group, the growing family of galaxies that includes the Milky Way.

An irregular galaxy has no clear spiral or elliptical shape, and a starburst galaxy is one making new stars much faster than usual. Wolf-Rayet stars are very hot, massive stars that drive powerful winds and are shedding their outer layers, a short phase late in their lives. Finding many young stars alongside them fits a galaxy in the middle of an energetic burst of star birth.
explore: The data were obtained with the Mosaic II camera on the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope at Kitt Peak, by P. Massey, G. Jacoby, K. Olsen and C. Smith; Travis Rector, Mahdi Zamani and Davide de Martin processed the image.

understand.summary: The Mosaic II camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope observed IC 10 through U, B, V, R and I filters plus narrow oxygen (O III), hydrogen-alpha and sulphur (S II) filters, from near-ultraviolet to the edge of near-infrared; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: Narrowband filters single out light from glowing gas, and long exposures gather far more light than the eye, so faint star-forming regions become visible.

scaleExtra: IC 10 lies around 2 million light-years from Earth, according to NOIRLab.
alt: An irregular galaxy with many bright young stars.

caption: The interacting galaxies NGC 6872 and IC 4970, imaged by the Gemini South telescope
story: Two galaxies are caught in a gravitational embrace in this image from Gemini South. NGC 6872 is on the left, and its companion, IC 4970, is on the right. The pair is seen toward the constellation Pavo, the Peacock, at a distance of about 200 million light-years.

The two are interacting: each galaxy's gravity pulls on the other, and over time that tug can reshape both of them. Interactions like this often draw stars and gas out into long arms or streams, and they can squeeze gas clouds hard enough to start new bursts of star formation.

Many galaxies go through encounters of this kind, and some eventually merge. Studying pairs caught partway through the process helps astronomers understand how galaxies grow and change shape over their long lives.
explore: The image was made with Gemini South's GMOS-S instrument. Besides the Australian Gemini Office, its full credit names Travis Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage), the Sydney Girls High School Astronomy Club and Ángel López-Sánchez, from the Australian Astronomical Observatory and Macquarie University.

understand.summary: GMOS-S on Gemini South imaged the pair through g, r and i filters, covering visible and near-infrared light; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: At about 200 million light-years these galaxies are far too faint for the eye; the i filter also records near-infrared light we cannot see.

scaleExtra: The two galaxies lie about 200 million light-years away, according to Gemini Observatory.
alt: Two galaxies interacting, NGC 6872 on the left and its companion IC 4970 on the right.

caption: The Coma Cluster of galaxies, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope
story: Thousands of galaxies fill this view, some belonging to the Coma Cluster itself and others lying far behind it. The image was taken with the Dark Energy Camera. The cluster takes its name from the hair of the Egyptian queen Berenice II, a figure who also appears in Greek mythology, and it lies about 320 million light-years away.

The Coma Cluster was fundamental to the discovery of dark matter. In 1937, the Swiss astronomer Fritz Zwicky noticed that its galaxies behaved as though huge quantities of matter were pulling on them, matter that could not be seen. That unseen material is what we now call dark matter.

A galaxy cluster is a huge collection of galaxies bound together by gravity. The speeds of the galaxies inside it reveal how much mass is holding the cluster together, and in Coma that mass far exceeds what the visible galaxies account for.
explore: The full image can be explored in a zoomable version, which lets visitors pan across the thousands of cluster and background galaxies it contains.

understand.summary: The Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope observed the Coma Cluster through g, r, i and z filters, covering visible and near-infrared light; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: These galaxies are far too faint to see with the eye, and the z filter records near-infrared light that is invisible to us.

alt: A wide field of many galaxies.

caption: The Sombrero Galaxy, Messier 104, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope
story: This image shows Messier 104, also catalogued as NGC 4594 and nicknamed the Sombrero Galaxy, in the constellation Virgo. Its familiar features are both here: an extended halo and a disc filled with dust.
The Sombrero is a popular target both for amateur observers and for professional research. Its nickname comes from its resemblance to a broad-brimmed hat, with the dusty disc forming the brim.

Dust in a galaxy's disc absorbs and blocks the light of stars behind it, which is why a dusty disc seen at an angle appears as a dark band. A galaxy's halo is a faint, extended region of stars surrounding the main body. Imaging both at once calls for a camera that can capture a wide field and also record faint light, and this view captures both.
explore: The image was taken with the Dark Energy Camera, a DOE-built instrument mounted on the NSF's Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope, which stands at Chile's Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory and is part of NSF NOIRLab. A cropped close-up version is also available.

understand.summary: The Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope observed the Sombrero through g, r and i filters and a narrowband N662 filter, covering visible and near-infrared light; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 1566, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope
story: The spiral galaxy NGC 1566 seems to twirl in this image, flinging its arms out into space. Nicknamed the Spanish Dancer, it lies about 20 million light-years away in the constellation Dorado.

Astronomers often turn to NGC 1566 when studying galaxy groups, stars of different ages and the black holes found in galaxies. A galaxy group is a small gathering of galaxies bound together by gravity, and seeing how members affect one another helps explain how galaxies change over time.

A spiral galaxy is a flat, rotating disc of stars, gas and dust. Its arms are where gas collects and new stars form, while older stars are spread more evenly through the disc and the central bulge. Most large galaxies are thought to have a massive black hole at their centre, and spirals like this one let astronomers study that region.
explore: The image was taken with the Dark Energy Camera, built by the US Department of Energy, on Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory's Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope, a Program of NSF NOIRLab. It is credited to the Dark Energy Survey.

understand.summary: The Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope observed NGC 1566 through g, r, i, z and Y filters, spanning visible and near-infrared light; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: The z and Y filters record near-infrared light that the eye cannot see, and the camera gathers far more light than an eye could.

caption: The Large Magellanic Cloud from the SMASH survey, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope
story: This image comes from the SMASH survey and gives a wide-angle view of the Large Magellanic Cloud unlike any before. The lower part of the image shows how deep the survey goes: a great many stars appear even in the galaxy's outer regions.

Of all the galaxies orbiting the Milky Way, the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds are the biggest. Unlike the other galaxies that orbit ours, they are still actively forming stars, and doing so at a rapid pace.

A satellite galaxy is a smaller galaxy that orbits a larger one, bound to it by gravity. Most of the Milky Way's satellites are small and have largely stopped making new stars, which makes the two Magellanic Clouds stand out. Mapping the faint outskirts of the Large Magellanic Cloud helps astronomers trace how far its stars extend and how it has been shaped by its larger neighbour.
explore: The data were gathered with the Dark Energy Camera on the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope. The SMASH data are credited to D. Nidever of Montana State University.

understand.summary: The Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope observed the Large Magellanic Cloud through g, r, i and z filters, covering visible and near-infrared light; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: The survey's deep exposures gather far more light than the eye, resolving a great many individual stars, even in the galaxy's outer regions.

alt: A wide view of the Large Magellanic Cloud, with many stars scattered through its outer regions at the bottom.

caption: The interacting galaxies NGC 1512 and NGC 1510, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope
story: Two galaxies take centre stage in this image: NGC 1512 and its smaller neighbour NGC 1510, a pair caught in the act of interacting, in the constellation Horologium.
NGC 1512 has been merging with NGC 1510 for 400 million years. That long, slow interaction has set off waves of star formation and bent both galaxies out of shape.

When galaxies interact, their gravity pulls on each other's stars and gas. Clouds of gas get compressed, and compressed gas is where new stars form, so encounters like this often trigger bursts of star birth. The same forces can distort a galaxy's disc, twisting or warping it. Over enough time, a smaller galaxy can be absorbed entirely by a larger one, and mergers of this kind are thought to be one of the main ways galaxies grow.
explore: The image was taken with the Dark Energy Camera, a wide-field imager on Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory's Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope, a Program of NSF NOIRLab. It is credited to the Dark Energy Survey.

understand.summary: The Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope observed the pair through g, r, i, z and Y filters, covering visible and near-infrared light; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: The z and Y filters capture near-infrared light the eye cannot see, and the camera gathers far more light than an eye could.
