caption: The irregular dwarf galaxy IC 1613, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope
story: This view shows the irregular dwarf galaxy IC 1613. To its lower right sits a distant galaxy cluster, dozens of orange-yellow blobs gathered around a pair of giant elliptical galaxies. To its left shines a bright foreground star in our own Milky Way, recognisable by its sharp diffraction spikes.

IC 1613 holds some 100 million stars and belongs to our Local Group of galaxies, along with the Milky Way, the Andromeda spiral and the Magellanic Clouds. It lies 2.4 million light-years away. Most of its stars formed about 7 billion years ago, and unlike very active dwarf irregulars such as the Magellanic Clouds, it does not appear to be forming stars today.
It also contains several Cepheid variable stars. Cepheids pulse in brightness in a regular way that reveals their true brightness, making them key calibrators for measuring cosmic distances.
explore: The background cluster is several hundred times farther away than IC 1613. The bright foreground star, of sixth magnitude, lies in the constellation Cetus, the Whale, and its spikes radiate at 45-degree angles.

This view is a small piece of the Dark Energy Survey, a global collaboration including Fermilab, NCSA and NSF NOIRLab, which released a huge public collection of data from six years of work, all taken with DOE's Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope.

understand.summary: The Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope observed IC 1613 in visible and near-infrared light through G, R and I filters; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: The foreground star's spikes are not real: they are diffraction spikes, created as light bends around structures inside the telescope, something the eye would not see looking at the sky.

scaleExtra: IC 1613 lies 2.4 million light-years away, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A loose irregular galaxy of stars, with a small cluster of orange-yellow galaxies at lower right and a bright spiked star to the left.

caption: The Great Barred Spiral Galaxy, NGC 1365, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope
story: A prominent bar crosses the middle of NGC 1365, along with graceful spiral arms and lanes of dust dimming the broad, diffuse glow of stars. Also known as the Great Barred Spiral Galaxy, it belongs to the Fornax Cluster of galaxies and is a strikingly clean example of its type.
The central bar affects star formation throughout the whole galaxy. It also hides a supermassive black hole, concealed behind crowds of newly formed stars.

Barred spirals like NGC 1365 interest astronomers for more than their looks. Our own Milky Way is also a barred spiral, and because we cannot see it from outside, galaxies like this one offer clues to how our home galaxy works. Studying NGC 1365 is, in a sense, a way of looking at ourselves from afar.
explore: The image uses data from the Dark Energy Survey, which mapped hundreds of millions of galaxies with the Dark Energy Camera on Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory's Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope.

The 570-megapixel camera, one of the best-performing wide-field CCD imagers in the world, was designed for the survey, funded by the DOE and built and tested at Fermilab. The DOE and NSF operated it for the survey from 2013 to 2019; it now serves many other science programs.

understand.summary: The Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope observed NGC 1365 through g, r and i filters, covering visible and near-infrared light; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: The i filter reaches into near-infrared light the eye cannot see, and the survey's exposures gather far more light than an eye could.

alt: A barred spiral galaxy with a strong central bar, sweeping spiral arms and dark dust lanes.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 6744, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope
story: A luminous core sits at the centre of NGC 6744, surrounded by spiral arms that span 175,000 light-years. At the lower right, at the end of one arm, is a faint blob: its companion galaxy, NGC 6744A. On the left, a faint extended arm is visible, a feature rarely seen in most images.

Found in the constellation Pavo, NGC 6744 lies around 30 million light-years away. Its anatomy resembles that of our own Milky Way, only larger, and even its companion echoes ours: the pairing is similar to the one between the Milky Way and the Large Magellanic Cloud, its dwarf companion.
Nobody can step outside the Milky Way to photograph it. Galaxies like NGC 6744 give astronomers a stand-in, offering a sense of how our home might look to an observer far away.
explore: Few images of NGC 6744 have ever gone this deep. It was made with the Dark Energy Camera on Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory's Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope in Chile. The image belongs to the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys, an effort to build the largest 3D map of the night sky.

understand.summary: The Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope observed NGC 6744 in visible light through g and r filters and a hydrogen-alpha filter; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: The deep exposures reveal the faint outer arm and companion galaxy, which would be far too dim for the eye to see through a telescope.

alt: A large spiral galaxy with a bright core and wide arms, with a faint small companion galaxy at lower right.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 7331, imaged by the Gemini North telescope
story: Dark lanes of dust wind through the spiral arms of NGC 7331, threaded among populations of hot stars. Found in the constellation Pegasus, approximately 40 million light-years away, this galaxy is the brightest and nearest member of the group of galaxies named after it, the NGC 7331 Group.

Also known as Caldwell 30, NGC 7331 is often described as a twin of the Milky Way, because it is similar in size and has a comparable spiral structure. Its core, though, sets it apart from our home galaxy in a couple of ways.

There is evidence that a bar of stars and dust cuts across the middle of the Milky Way, a feature shared by many spiral galaxies. NGC 7331 has no such bar. Stranger still, its central bulge spins the opposite way from its disc, which is unusual among galaxies and not what astronomers see in our own Galaxy.
explore: This image was taken with Gemini North, half of the International Gemini Observatory. The observatory is supported in part by the US National Science Foundation and operated by NSF NOIRLab. Earlier views of NGC 7331, taken at Kitt Peak National Observatory in 1975 and 2014, can be found in the NOIRLab image archive.

understand.summary: Gemini North's GMOS-N instrument imaged NGC 7331 through g, r and i filters, covering visible and near-infrared light; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: The i filter records near-infrared light the eye cannot see, and the telescope gathers far more light than an eye, revealing the fine dust lanes.

alt: A spiral galaxy with a bright core, its arms laced with dark dust lanes and hot stars.

caption: The peculiar galaxy NGC 922, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope
story: An umbrella-shaped tidal tail spreads out from NGC 922 in this image, a feature only recently detected. The peculiar galaxy lies in the southern constellation Fornax, about 140 million light-years away, and its structure has puzzled astronomers for years.

Its distinctive features, a plume of stars and a galactic bar that sits off-centre, were once blamed on a collision, some 330 million years ago, with a dwarf galaxy nearby. The new observations challenge that story. The newly seen tail does not line up with the path of the dwarf galaxy, and the dwarf itself is still forming stars and has a well-defined shape, which does not fit the aftermath of a direct hit.
So a new idea has emerged: NGC 922 may have merged with a stripped dwarf galaxy, one that had already lost much of its material in earlier encounters with other galaxies.
explore: As scientists rewrite the galaxy's history, its tidal features make NGC 922 a valuable case for understanding how galaxies develop after interactions. The image was taken with the DOE-built Dark Energy Camera on the NSF's Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory.

understand.summary: The Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope observed NGC 922 through g, r and z filters, covering visible and near-infrared light; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: The faint tidal tail is far too dim to see by eye; deep exposures and a z filter reaching into invisible near-infrared light bring it out.

alt: A distorted galaxy with an off-centre bar and an umbrella-shaped tail of stars spreading from it.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 1398, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope
story: NGC 1398 shows off a bright central bar and delicate spiral arms, a barred spiral galaxy that seems to drift alone in a field of stars. Its home on the sky is the constellation Fornax, roughly 65 million light-years from Earth.

Look more closely, though, and the galaxy is far from alone. The sky around it is full of the smudges and swirls of distant galaxies, far beyond NGC 1398. This deep portrait captures the galaxy and its surroundings together.

In a barred spiral, a straight band of stars crosses the centre, and the spiral arms begin near its ends. Deep images like this one, covering a wide field, let astronomers study one galaxy in detail while also recording huge numbers of much more distant galaxies in the same frame.
explore: The image was taken with Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory's Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope. In 1995 the telescope was named in honour of Víctor Manuel Blanco, a Puerto Rican astronomer who became the observatory's second director. It was captured for the DOE-funded Dark Energy Survey using DECam, built and tested at Fermilab.

understand.summary: The Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope observed NGC 1398 through g, r and i filters, covering visible and near-infrared light; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: The distant background galaxies are far too faint for the eye; the survey's deep exposures reveal them, and the i filter reaches into near-infrared light.

alt: A barred spiral galaxy with a bright bar and delicate arms, surrounded by stars and many small, faint distant galaxies.

caption: The Milky Way rising over the summit of Maunakea, Hawaiʻi
story: Rising in the east, the disc of the Milky Way spreads along the horizon over the summit of Maunakea in Hawaiʻi. The centre of our Galaxy stands behind the Maunakea Observatories, whose silhouettes include Gemini North, third from the left.

Maunakea lies about 19 degrees north of the equator, one of the most southerly spots in the United States, so from there a large part of the southern sky can be seen. At the centre of the photograph is the constellation Scorpius, with its bright red heart, the star Antares. Ophiuchus lies to its left, and both are dotted with colourful nebulae.

On the right are three famous sights. Centaurus can be found by its bright yellow front hoof, Alpha Centauri, a triple star system that includes Proxima Centauri, the closest star to the Sun. Below it is Crux, the Cross, which points toward the south pole. The red spot to its right is the Carina Nebula.
explore: Crux is marked by a red star at its top and a triangle of blue stars below, and it has long been a key navigation aid in the southern hemisphere. The Carina Nebula, NGC 3372, ranks among the largest diffuse nebulae seen from Earth and is intensely studied for the many objects inside it.
The photo was taken during the NOIRLab 2022 Photo Expedition to all NOIRLab sites by Tomáš Slovinský, a NOIRLab Audiovisual Ambassador.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken with a camera in visible light from Maunakea; the camera settings and processing are not published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers far more light than the eye, so the Milky Way's glow and the colours of its nebulae look far richer than they would to someone on the summit.

alt: The Milky Way rises above a mountain summit with silhouetted observatory domes, with a red nebula and bright stars scattered along it.

caption: The needle-thin galaxy IC 2233, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope at Kitt Peak
story: The remarkably thin galaxy IC 2233 is the subject of this image, its profile as slender as a needle. Its slender profile comes from two things together: its structure and the way it is oriented toward Earth.

Astronomers call a galaxy's tilt its inclination, and IC 2233 is seen almost exactly edge-on, which makes it one of the flattest galaxies known. It also lacks the prominent central bulge that thickens the profile of spirals such as Andromeda and the Milky Way. The exposure is deep, and the whole field is scattered with other galaxies tilted at all sorts of angles.

The galaxy's wafer-thin shape has intrigued observers for nearly 150 years. It was discovered in 1874 by Isaac Roberts, a Welsh amateur astronomer who was one of the pioneers of photographing the sky.
explore: The image was taken with Kitt Peak National Observatory's Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope, part of NSF NOIRLab, using the Mosaic I camera. IC 2233 lies in the constellation Lynx.

understand.summary: The Mosaic I camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope observed IC 2233 through U, B and R filters plus a hydrogen-alpha filter, spanning near-ultraviolet and visible light; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: The deep exposure gathers far more light than the eye, revealing the many faint background galaxies that fill the field.

alt: A very thin, edge-on galaxy, surrounded by many other galaxies in the field.

caption: The Small Magellanic Cloud from the SMASH survey, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope
story: This image, part of the SMASH survey, offers what may be the finest wide-angle view yet of the Small Magellanic Cloud, one of our Galaxy's closest companions.
Of all the galaxies orbiting the Milky Way, the two Magellanic Clouds are the biggest. They also differ from the rest in that both are still busily making new stars, and quickly.

A satellite galaxy is a smaller galaxy that orbits a larger one, held by its gravity. The rest of the Milky Way's satellites are no longer actively forming stars, which is why the two Magellanic Clouds stand out. A galaxy that is still making stars keeps a supply of gas and dust, and the young stars born from it are often hot and bright. Wide, deep surveys like this one let astronomers study huge numbers of individual stars across a whole galaxy in a single consistent set of images, which helps them piece together how and when its stars formed.
explore: The data were taken with the Dark Energy Camera on the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope, and the SMASH data are credited to D. Nidever of Montana State University.

understand.summary: The Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope observed the Small Magellanic Cloud through g, r, i and z filters, covering visible and near-infrared light; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: The survey's deep exposures gather far more light than the eye, resolving the galaxy into individual stars.

alt: A wide view of the Small Magellanic Cloud.

caption: The flocculent spiral galaxy NGC 7793, imaged by the Gemini South telescope
story: This observation from the International Gemini Observatory shows NGC 7793, a flocculent spiral galaxy in the constellation Sculptor, nearly 12 million light-years away.

Flocculent means fluffy or woolly, and it describes the oddly tufted look of galaxies like this one. Instead of the long, elegant arms of a spiral such as Andromeda, a flocculent galaxy has short, patchy segments of arms that give it a soft, cottony appearance.

Sculptor lies close to the south Galactic pole, so objects in it, NGC 7793 included, are well placed for telescopes in Earth's southern hemisphere such as Gemini South. From its mountaintop site in the Chilean Andes, Gemini South has a fine view of many intriguing southern-sky objects, including NGC 7793, the Magellanic Clouds and the centre of the Milky Way. Looking toward the Galactic pole also means looking away from the dusty disc of our own Galaxy, giving a clearer view of objects beyond.
explore: The image was made with the GMOS-S instrument on Gemini South, part of the International Gemini Observatory, operated by NSF NOIRLab.

understand.summary: GMOS-S on Gemini South imaged NGC 7793 through g, r and i filters, covering visible and near-infrared light; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: The i filter records near-infrared light the eye cannot see, and the telescope gathers far more light, bringing out the galaxy's tufted texture.

alt: A spiral galaxy with patchy, tufted arms instead of clearly defined long ones.

caption: The galaxy pair NGC 672 and IC 1727, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope at Kitt Peak
story: Two galaxies seem almost to elbow each other in this image: NGC 672 at the top right and IC 1727 at the bottom left. They are classed as a galactic pair, meaning the gravity of each one affects the other.

The pair lies around 20 million light-years from Earth, in the constellation Triangulum. The gap between them spans more than 80,000 light-years, which sounds enormous. From the galaxies' own point of view, however, it is not so large, since that separation is roughly the same as the size of the galaxies themselves.

Gravitational interactions between neighbouring galaxies can gradually reshape them, pulling on their stars and gas and stirring up clouds that may go on to form new stars. Pairs like this one give astronomers a chance to study galaxies that are influencing each other.
explore: The image comes from NSF Kitt Peak National Observatory, part of NSF NOIRLab, with the Mosaic I camera on the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope.

understand.summary: The Mosaic I camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope observed the pair through U, B and R filters plus a hydrogen-alpha filter, spanning near-ultraviolet and visible light; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: Long exposures on a large telescope gather far more light than the eye could.

caption: The collision-ringed galaxy NGC 5291 and the Seashell, imaged by the SMARTS 0.9-meter Telescope at Cerro Tololo
story: At the centre of this image is a hazy, golden oval: the elliptical galaxy NGC 5291. Faint, glowing clouds spread out to its left and right, forming a ring of debris left behind by a violent galactic collision.

More than 300 million years ago, NGC 5291 was struck by a rogue galaxy hurtling through space. The debris ring is the aftermath of that impact. NGC 5291 lies about 200 million light-years away, in the constellation Centaurus.

The image also shows a much gentler encounter. Just to the right of NGC 5291 is an unusually curved galaxy known as the Seashell, and the two are interacting calmly with each other. An elliptical galaxy is a smooth, rounded collection of stars without spiral arms, and collisions like this one show how violently such galaxies can be disturbed.
explore: Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory's SMARTS 0.9-meter Telescope made the observation.

understand.summary: The SMARTS 0.9-meter Telescope at Cerro Tololo observed NGC 5291 through u, g, r and i filters, from near-ultraviolet through visible light to the edge of near-infrared; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: The faint debris clouds are far too dim for the eye; the camera's exposures gather enough light to reveal them.

caption: Vera C. Rubin Observatory under the Milky Way, Cerro Pachón
story: The NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory sits beneath the dense tangle of gas and dust of the Milky Way, its dome open. From behind Cerro Pachón, the mountain it calls home, peek faint blue and red hints of airglow, which blend into the warm glow of city lights from La Serena.

Airglow is a faint light given off by energised atoms in Earth's upper atmosphere. The open dome means Rubin is ready to survey the southern sky with the LSST Camera, a 3200-megapixel instrument that is the largest digital camera in the world, roughly as big as an SUV, with a weight of around 3000 kg.

Rubin can record very faint objects that give off or reflect little light, such as ultra diffuse galaxies: systems as large as the Milky Way but with only a hundredth to a thousandth as many stars. Studying them lets scientists test ideas about dark matter and learn how galaxies grow, interact and collide.
explore: The photographer, Hernán Stockebrand, is a DevOps engineer at Rubin Observatory and a NOIRLab Audiovisual Ambassador. Rubin is jointly funded by the US National Science Foundation and the Department of Energy's Office of Science, and is operated jointly by NSF NOIRLab and DOE's SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory.

understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers much more light than the eye, so faint airglow and the Milky Way's dust show up more strongly than they would to someone standing there.

caption: The Milky Way and the Rho Ophiuchi cloud complex, near Cerro Pachón, Chile
story: The Milky Way's glowing disc stretches across this sky near Cerro Pachón in Chile, partly hidden by dark interstellar dust clouds known as the Great Rift. Some fragments of these dark nebulae seem to reach toward a small cluster of colour: the Rho Ophiuchi cloud complex.

That complex mixes reflection nebulae, which scatter blue and yellow light from nearby stars, with emission nebulae, which shine with the reddish light of hot hydrogen gas. Tucked inside it are the star Rho Ophiuchi and Antares, the heart of Scorpius. Above the group lies a much larger deep red emission nebula, Sh2-27, surrounding the star Zeta Ophiuchi.

The soft light to the right of centre is the gegenschein: sunlight bounced back by dust particles in the outer Solar System. That dust, which also produces the zodiacal light, comes from sources that include comet tails and collisions between asteroids.
explore: Cerro Pachón is home to several NSF NOIRLab facilities, among them the SOAR Telescope, Vera C. Rubin Observatory and half of the International Gemini Observatory. This 170-megapixel photograph was taken during the NOIRLab 2022 Photo Expedition by P. Horálek of the Institute of Physics in Opava, and can be explored with a zoom feature.

understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers much more light than the eye, so the colours of the nebulae and the faint gegenschein appear far more clearly than they would to the naked eye.

caption: Gemini South and Vera C. Rubin Observatory at night, Cerro Pachón
story: Gemini South, which makes up half of the International Gemini Observatory, stands on Cerro Pachón in this night photograph. Behind it rises the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which has just begun operating.

The photograph's theme is speed. A meteor may be visible for only a few seconds, and many astronomical objects change quickly. Studying these fleeting changes is called time-domain astronomy, and Gemini is often one of the observatories that follows up on fast-changing events: supernovae, asteroids, variable stars, active galactic nuclei and meteors. In 2025, Gemini South follow-up helped astronomers characterise the nearest supernova known to be tied to a fast X-ray transient, as well as the near-Earth asteroid 2024 YR4.

Rubin works hand in hand with this kind of follow-up. As a survey telescope, it will sweep the southern sky and pick up as many as 10 million changes each night, with every one triggering an alert to astronomers within minutes.
explore: Rubin is jointly funded by the US National Science Foundation and the Department of Energy's Office of Science. A fulldome version of the photograph is also available. The photographer, Petr Horálek, is a NOIRLab Audiovisual Ambassador.

caption: The Milky Way over Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory, Chile
story: The slanting arms of our Galaxy stretch over a row of telescopes at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory, in the foothills of the Chilean Andes. The centre of the Milky Way seems to set the whole band alight, shining with the light of millions of stars even though clouds of interstellar dust block part of it.

From the southern hemisphere, where the observatory sits, Earth's orientation lets observers take in most of the Milky Way on a clear night. From our vantage point, the heart of the Galaxy lies in the direction of the constellations Sagittarius, Ophiuchus and Scorpius. At its very core is a supermassive black hole known as Sagittarius A*.
NOIRLab describes the view from these foothills as some of the best night-sky viewing in the world, and the observatory's telescopes aim to make the most of it.
explore: From left to right, the buildings beneath the Milky Way are the US Naval Observatory Deep South Telescope, the DIMM1 Seeing Monitor, the dome of the CHilean Automatic Supernova sEarch, aTmCam (straight back), the SMARTS 1.0-meter Telescope, the UBC Southern Observatory and the Curtis Schmidt Telescope. This 250-megapixel photograph was taken by T. Slovinský during the NOIRLab 2022 Photo Expedition.

caption: NGC 6240, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope
story: This is a detailed image of NGC 6240, a galaxy in the direction of the constellation Ophiuchus, taken with the Dark Energy Camera, or DECam.

The US Department of Energy built DECam, and it sits on Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory's Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope in Chile, part of NSF NOIRLab. It is a wide-field camera, designed to photograph large areas of sky in a single exposure while still picking up faint objects.

For this picture it recorded light through three filters, known as g, r and z. The g and r filters cover parts of the visible spectrum, while z reaches into near-infrared light just beyond what human eyes can see. Combining separate exposures like these is how astronomers build a colour image: each filter is assigned a colour, and together they approximate the full picture. Observing across several wavelengths also helps astronomers compare how different kinds of stars, gas and dust contribute to a galaxy's light.

caption: A fireball over Gemini North, Hawaiʻi
story: A blazing rock streaks through the atmosphere in the pale orange sky above Gemini North, caught by one of the telescope's cloud cameras. Gemini North makes up half of the International Gemini Observatory, which NSF NOIRLab operates with partial funding from the US National Science Foundation.

The streak over Hawaiʻi Island is a meteor, or shooting star. This one is a special kind called a fireball, named for how bright it is. The American Meteor Society defines a fireball as a meteor that looks brighter than Venus does in the morning or evening sky to someone on Earth.

Fireballs can occasionally make striking sounds as they pass through the air. If an exceptionally bright one explodes in the stratosphere, people on the ground may hear a sonic boom, even in daytime. So anyone keen to wish on a shooting star can, in principle, look or listen for one during the day as well.
explore: Cloud cameras like the one that caught this fireball keep watch over the sky at observatory sites. NOIRLab has collected other fireballs captured around its Program sites.

understand.summary: This picture comes from a Gemini North cloud camera, a camera that watches the sky above the telescope in visible light; its settings are not published.
understand.eye: A bright fireball is visible to the eye, but only for a moment; the camera records its full path as a single streak.

alt: A bright meteor streaks across a pale orange sky above Gemini North.

caption: The irregular galaxy NGC 6822, imaged by the Blanco 4-meter Telescope
story: Countless hot, blue, massive stars and several well-known nebulae stand out in this colour image of NGC 6822, a nearby irregular galaxy. Found in the constellation Sagittarius, approximately 1.6 million light-years from Earth, it is a member of the Local Group, the family of galaxies that includes the Milky Way.

E. E. Barnard discovered NGC 6822 in the early 1880s. Edwin P. Hubble made the first detailed study of it in 1925, with the then-new 100-inch telescope on Mount Wilson. In 1966 Susan E. Kayser, then a graduate student, analysed those photographic plates, and her work remained the most complete study of the galaxy until these new observations.

An irregular galaxy has no clear spiral or elliptical form. The many blue massive stars here are young, since such stars burn out quickly, which tells astronomers that NGC 6822 has formed stars recently.
explore: The images were taken in eight filters with the Blanco 4-meter telescope at Cerro Tololo, near La Serena, Chile, by CTIO staff Knut Olsen and Chris Smith, part of the Local Group Galaxies Survey Team led by Phil Massey of Lowell Observatory. The survey was one of 13 active survey projects supported by the National Optical Astronomy Observatory.

understand.summary: The Blanco 4-meter telescope's Mosaic II camera observed NGC 6822 in eight filters; Travis Rector combined seven of them, with U shown as violet, B as blue, V as green, R as orange, I as red, hydrogen-alpha as red and oxygen (O III) as blue.
understand.eye: The U filter records near-ultraviolet light the eye barely sees, and narrow hydrogen and oxygen filters pick out glowing nebulae far too faint to see directly.

scaleExtra: NGC 6822 lies approximately 1.6 million light-years from Earth, according to NOIRLab.
alt: An irregular galaxy full of blue stars, with several glowing nebulae.

caption: The globular cluster Omega Centauri, imaged by NEWFIRM on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope
story: This infrared image shows Omega Centauri, the largest globular cluster in the Milky Way, packed with approximately 10 million stars. Seen toward the constellation Centaurus, it is about 17,000 light-years from Earth.

The picture was taken while NEWFIRM, an infrared camera on Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory's Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope in Chile, was being commissioned and put through capability tests. Its size and richness make Omega Centauri a popular target for such observations.

A globular cluster is a dense, roughly spherical swarm of old stars bound together by gravity. Observing in infrared light has particular advantages for a cluster like this: infrared passes through dust more easily than visible light, and many of the cool, old stars that fill globular clusters shine strongly at these longer wavelengths. Testing a new camera on such a crowded field also shows how well it can separate stars packed close together.
explore: Commissioning is the period when a new instrument is installed and tested on a telescope before it begins regular science observations.

understand.summary: NEWFIRM on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope observed Omega Centauri in near-infrared light through J, H and Ks filters; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the human eye, so the colours here are a translation of wavelengths we cannot see.

scaleExtra: Omega Centauri is about 17,000 light-years from Earth, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A huge, dense globular cluster of stars.

caption: A fireball above Gemini North, Maunakea, Hawaiʻi
story: An extra-bright meteor, known as a fireball, flashes across the sky in this frame from a live webcam on Maunakea, Hawaiʻi, close to the Gemini North telescope. Gemini North makes up half of the International Gemini Observatory, which NSF NOIRLab operates with partial funding from the US National Science Foundation.
Live webcams at observing sites are usually there to keep an eye on the weather. Because they are always watching, though, they can also catch brief events in the sky, like this one.

Fireballs are meteors that are brighter than average, so bright that they can even be seen during the day. The American Meteor Society has recorded a steadily rising number of them each year. In fact, several thousand fireballs happen every day, but most go unnoticed: the majority occur over the ocean, and half take place in daylight.
explore: The same webcam also recorded this fireball as part of a time-lapse image of the night sky over Maunakea, which NOIRLab has published alongside this frame.

understand.summary: This picture comes from the Maunakea live webcam near Gemini North, which records the sky in visible light; its settings are not published.
understand.eye: A fireball is bright enough to see with the eye, but it lasts only moments; the webcam preserves it as a single image.

alt: A bright meteor streaks across the night sky near the Gemini North telescope.

caption: The disturbed spiral galaxy NGC 5474, imaged at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center
story: Pink star-forming regions and blue clusters of young stars are sprinkled along the spiral structure of NGC 5474, a lopsided galaxy in Ursa Major. Its slightly grainy look comes from the camera partly resolving some of the brighter individual stars in the disc.

NGC 5474 is being strongly disturbed by its much larger neighbour, M101, which lies several fields of view beyond this image toward the upper left. At first glance it looks as if M101 is dragging the galaxy's nucleus right out of it. Computer models tell a slightly different story. Using tens or even hundreds of thousands of point masses to stand in for stars, astronomers found that the lopsidedness is probably fairly brief; we just happen to catch the galaxy in a sloshed, agitated state.

How long it lasts depends on how NGC 5474 orbits M101 compared with how its disc spins. When the two run in opposite directions, as here, the lopsided shape can persist for many rotations after a strong initial tidal disturbance.
explore: This image was taken by Adam Block in 2014 as part of the Advanced Observing Program at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center, using a CCD camera at the Visitor Center's roll-off roof observatory.

understand.summary: A CCD camera at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center's roll-off roof observatory recorded NGC 5474 in visible light through B, G, R and broadband filters; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: The camera's exposures reveal pink and blue star-forming regions and individual bright stars that would be invisible to the eye at the telescope.

alt: A lopsided spiral galaxy with an off-centre core, dotted with pink and blue patches along its arms.

caption: The starburst galaxy M82, imaged by the WIYN 3.5-meter telescope and the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This colour-coded picture shows M82, the archetypal starburst galaxy. Its stellar disc runs horizontally across the image and is where its intense star formation takes place. Rising perpendicular to the disc is a galactic superwind of ionised gas, driven by the energy released by the burst of star birth.

A starburst galaxy forms stars much faster than usual. So many massive young stars live and die so quickly that their combined winds and explosions blast gas out of the galaxy, producing the outflow seen here. Dust lanes are visible in the central part of the superwind on both sides of the disc, shown at varying angular resolution.

That mix of resolutions comes from the data sources. The image merges observations made by Kitt Peak's WIYN 3.5-meter telescope with data from Hubble's WFPC2 camera. The data are being used to study how structures within M82 connect to its superwind.
explore: The image was first shown at the Essential Science in Hubble's Final Years symposium, held at the Space Telescope Science Institute in May 2004. Kitt Peak's WIYN 3.5-meter and 0.9-meter telescopes are run by a consortium: the University of Wisconsin, Indiana University and Yale University, together with the National Optical Astronomy Observatory.

understand.summary: The image combines WIYN 3.5-meter and Hubble WFPC2 data in visible light. In the WIYN data, purple shows glowing hydrogen (hydrogen-alpha) together with ionised nitrogen, and green shows ionised sulphur; in the Hubble data these colours show hydrogen-alpha and nitrogen separately.
understand.eye: The colours are coded to particular glowing gases rather than showing natural colour, so the superwind stands out in a way the eye would never see.

alt: A horizontal galaxy disc with a purple and green outflow of gas rising above and below it, laced with dark dust.

caption: The star-forming region NGC 206 in the Andromeda Galaxy, imaged by the WIYN 0.9-meter telescope
story: A bluish patch of stars sits between the centre and upper-left corner of this view of the Andromeda Galaxy, M31. This is NGC 206, a massive star-forming region embedded in Andromeda, of the kind called an OB association. Scattered red nebulae mark other places in the galaxy where stars are forming right now.
NGC 206 is estimated to contain about 200,000 times the mass of our Sun. Its distinctive blue colour comes from very young, hot and massive stars.

Those stars also reveal its age. Massive stars burn through their fuel quickly and do not last long, so their presence shows that the cluster has existed for less than 10 million years, extremely young for stars. An OB association is a loose grouping of these short-lived O and B type stars, born around the same time from the same region of gas.
explore: The image was obtained with the wide-field Mosaic camera on the WIYN 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory. It is oriented with north at the bottom and east to the right.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the WIYN 0.9-meter telescope observed this part of Andromeda in visible light through B, V and hydrogen-alpha filters, shown as blue, green and red respectively.
understand.eye: The hydrogen-alpha filter isolates the red glow of star-forming gas, bringing out nebulae that the eye could not pick out in the galaxy's overall light.

alt: Part of a spiral galaxy with a bright bluish cluster of stars near the centre to upper left and scattered small red nebulae.

caption: The Sculptor Galaxy, NGC 253, imaged by the Blanco 4-meter Telescope
story: This image shows the spiral galaxy NGC 253, also called the Sculptor Galaxy, one of the brightest galaxies that lies beyond our Local Group. Among the Sculptor group of galaxies it is the brightest member; the group clusters around the south galactic pole and is therefore sometimes called the South Polar Group.

Beyond our own Local Group, the Sculptor group may be the next nearest galaxy group, at about 8 million light-years from Earth. NGC 253 is considered a starburst galaxy, meaning that stars are born, and blow up, within it at an unusually high rate.
The galaxy also has an interesting place in history. It was one of the major discoveries of Caroline Herschel, sister of the astronomer William Herschel, who found it on 23 September 1783.
explore: The image was taken with the National Science Foundation's Blanco 4-meter telescope, at Chile's Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory, using the Mosaic II camera.

understand.summary: The Mosaic II camera on the Blanco 4-meter telescope observed NGC 253 through B, V and I filters plus a hydrogen-alpha filter, covering visible light to the edge of near-infrared; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: The camera's exposures gather far more light than the eye, and the I filter reaches toward near-infrared light.

scaleExtra: The Sculptor group is about 8 million light-years from Earth, according to NOIRLab.
alt: The spiral galaxy NGC 253, the Sculptor Galaxy.

caption: The peculiar barred spiral galaxy NGC 2146, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter telescope at Kitt Peak
story: The large galaxy in the lower-right corner of this image is NGC 2146, classified as a peculiar barred spiral. The smaller galaxy in the upper-left corner is NGC 2146A, which is likely a companion.

NGC 2146 also counts as a starburst galaxy, since it is making new stars quickly. It is likely the product of two galaxies that collided and are now near the end of merging into one. What part, if any, NGC 2146A has played in that star formation or merger history is unclear.

When galaxies collide, their gas clouds are squeezed and stirred, and compressed gas is where new stars are born, which is why mergers so often trigger starbursts. A peculiar galaxy is one whose shape does not fit the standard spiral or elliptical categories, often because of just this kind of disturbance. NGC 2146 lies in the constellation Camelopardalis.
explore: The image was obtained with the wide-field Mosaic camera of Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. North is up and east is to the left.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter telescope observed NGC 2146 through B, V, I and hydrogen-alpha filters, shown as blue, green, orange and red respectively.
understand.eye: The I filter reaches toward near-infrared light at the edge of human vision, and the hydrogen-alpha filter highlights glowing star-forming gas the eye would miss.

alt: A large, distorted spiral galaxy at lower right and a smaller galaxy at upper left.

caption: The Large Magellanic Cloud from the MCELS survey, imaged by the SMARTS 0.9-meter telescope
story: This large mosaic of the Large Magellanic Cloud was built from more than 1,500 individual images. It focuses on the glowing gas of the interstellar medium, the material that fills the space between the stars.

The interstellar medium plays two roles. It is the breeding ground where new stars form, and it is also the graveyard where the remains of dead stars eventually end up. The images come from the Magellanic Cloud Emission Line Survey, or MCELS, a study led by astronomers at the National Optical Astronomy Observatory that concentrated specifically on this gas in the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, the nearest major galaxies to the Milky Way.

An emission-line survey uses filters that let through only the particular colours of light given off by glowing gases such as hydrogen and sulphur. That makes the gas stand out sharply against the background of stars.
explore: The public first saw the mosaic in January 2006, when it was unveiled in Washington, DC, at the American Astronomical Society's annual meeting. It is credited to C. Smith, S. Points and the MCELS team.

understand.summary: A camera on the SMARTS 0.9-meter telescope observed the Large Magellanic Cloud through hydrogen-alpha, sulphur (S II) and G filters in visible light; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: The narrow filters isolate the light of glowing gas, making it stand out far more than it would to the eye.

alt: A wide mosaic of the Large Magellanic Cloud showing its glowing gas.

caption: The spiral galaxies NGC 3166 and NGC 3169, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter telescope at Kitt Peak
story: Two spiral galaxies are caught in a slow, fatal embrace in this image: NGC 3166 at the lower right and NGC 3169 at the upper left. As the pair begins to merge, the galaxies are starting to pull each other apart.

The faint wisps around NGC 3169 are its outer spiral arms being torn away by the gravity of its neighbour. In time, the pair will combine into one galaxy. A third, smaller galaxy, NGC 3165, sits just below NGC 3166 and belongs to the same group.

Mergers like this are thought to be one of the main ways galaxies grow. Over very long spans of time, gravity strips away stars and gas, reshapes the discs, and eventually blends two separate galaxies into one larger system. Catching a pair partway through the process shows the stages that are too slow for us to watch unfold. The galaxies lie in the constellation Sextans.
explore: The image was obtained with the wide-field Mosaic camera of Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. It is rotated 30 degrees clockwise from the usual orientation with north up and east to the left.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter telescope observed the galaxies through B, V, I and hydrogen-alpha filters, shown as blue, green, orange and red respectively.
understand.eye: The faint wisps of torn-off spiral arms are far too dim for the eye; long exposures on a large telescope bring them out.

alt: Two spiral galaxies, one at lower right and one at upper left surrounded by faint wisps, with a small galaxy below the lower one.

caption: The Hockey Stick Galaxy, NGC 4656, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter telescope at Kitt Peak
story: NGC 4656 is a spiral galaxy seen edge-on, but its disc is bent out of shape, giving it the look that earned it the informal nickname of the hockey stick galaxy. A faint object sits in the upper-left corner of the image.

The galaxy's unusual shape comes from a recent gravitational encounter with another galaxy, NGC 4631. The two may have begun to merge, though that is not yet certain. The faint object at the upper left may not belong to NGC 4656 at all; instead it may be a dwarf galaxy that is itself in the process of merging with it.

When galaxies pass close to each other, their gravity pulls on stars and gas, stretching and warping their discs. Seen edge-on, like this one, such distortions are especially easy to spot, because a normal disc would appear as a straight, thin line. NGC 4656 lies in the constellation Canes Venatici.
explore: The image was obtained with the wide-field Mosaic camera of Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. North is up and east is to the left.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter telescope observed NGC 4656 through B, V, I and hydrogen-alpha filters, shown as blue, green, orange and red respectively.
understand.eye: The I filter reaches toward near-infrared light at the edge of human vision, and the hydrogen-alpha filter highlights glowing gas the eye would not pick out.

alt: A distorted edge-on spiral galaxy, with a faint object in the upper-left corner.

caption: The galaxies M81 and M82, imaged by the KPNO 0.9-meter telescope
story: Two galaxies share this wide view: the spiral galaxy M81 on the left and M82 on the right. Filaments of red hydrogen gas stand out in M82, and just above M81, barely visible, is the very faint irregular dwarf galaxy Holmberg IX.

M81 and M82 are relatively nearby galaxies that are interacting through gravity. That interaction is making M82 form new stars at a massive rate, and the red hydrogen filaments are the evidence of it.

When galaxies pull on each other, clouds of gas get compressed and stirred, and dense gas is where stars are born. The glowing red hydrogen is gas lit up by the energy of hot young stars and the activity surrounding them. A dwarf irregular galaxy like Holmberg IX is a small system without a clear spiral or elliptical shape, and its faintness shows how much deeper the camera sees than the eye. The galaxies lie in the constellation Ursa Major.
explore: The image was obtained with the wide-field Mosaic camera on the 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory. It is oriented with north to the right and east at the top.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Kitt Peak 0.9-meter telescope observed the galaxies through B, V, R, I and hydrogen-alpha filters, shown as blue, cyan, green, orange and red respectively.
understand.eye: The hydrogen-alpha filter isolates the red glow of hydrogen, bringing out M82's filaments, and the I filter reaches toward near-infrared light the eye barely senses.

alt: A large spiral galaxy on the left and a galaxy with red filaments on the right, with a very faint small galaxy above the spiral.

caption: The dwarf galaxy NGC 4214, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter telescope at Kitt Peak
story: Many red clouds of hydrogen gas glow in NGC 4214, a dwarf galaxy much smaller than our own Milky Way. In the upper-right corner of the picture, its companion, the very small galaxy UGCA 276, is faintly visible.
Despite its small size, NGC 4214 is forming stars vigorously, and those red clouds are the sign of it.

The red glow comes from hydrogen gas energised by hot young stars forming inside the clouds, so each red patch marks a nursery of new stars. Dwarf galaxies are small, faint systems that often keep company with larger galaxies or, like NGC 4214, have even smaller companions of their own. Because they contain fewer stars and simpler structures than big spirals, they are useful for studying how star formation works in different conditions. Seeing a small galaxy so active shows that size alone does not decide how busy a galaxy can be. NGC 4214 lies in the constellation Canes Venatici.
explore: The image was obtained with the wide-field Mosaic camera of Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. It is rotated 55 degrees counterclockwise from the usual orientation with north up and east to the left.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter telescope observed NGC 4214 through B, V, I and hydrogen-alpha filters, shown as blue, cyan, orange and red respectively.
understand.eye: The hydrogen-alpha filter isolates the red light of glowing hydrogen, making star-forming clouds far more prominent than the eye could see.

alt: A dwarf galaxy dotted with red glowing clouds, with a very faint small galaxy in the upper-right corner.

caption: The globular cluster M15, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter telescope at Kitt Peak
story: This image shows M15, also catalogued as NGC 7078, a globular cluster in the constellation Pegasus that is estimated to hold more than 100,000 stars. Faint stars are recorded without the bright centre burning out to white.
That balance was a showcase for the new Mosaic 1.1 detectors, which could pick up faint stars without overexposing, or saturating, the bright heart of the cluster.

Hidden in the cluster is a planetary nebula called Pease 1. It appears blue and just slightly larger than a star, a small challenge for anyone scanning the image. A planetary nebula is a shell of gas thrown off by a Sun-like star near the end of its life, glowing because the hot core left behind lights it up. Finding one inside a globular cluster, a dense ball of old stars, is a reminder that its stars are still evolving.
explore: The image was obtained with the wide-field Mosaic camera of Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. It is oriented with north to the left and east at the bottom.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter telescope observed M15 through B, V and I filters, shown as blue, green and red respectively.
understand.eye: The I filter reaches toward near-infrared light the eye barely senses, and the detectors capture a range from faint outer stars to the bright core that the eye cannot take in at once.

alt: A dense ball of stars with a bright centre, containing a tiny blue nebula slightly larger than a star.

caption: The interacting galaxies NGC 4490 and NGC 4485, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter telescope at Kitt Peak
story: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 4490 sits at the centre of this image, with a smaller galaxy, NGC 4485, at the upper right. Bright red clouds of gas glow inside both galaxies and in the space between them.
The two are in the early stages of merging. Their mutual gravitational pull is triggering star formation in both galaxies, and those red clouds are where it is happening.

In a barred spiral, a straight band of stars crosses the centre and the spiral arms begin near its ends. When two galaxies interact, gravity squeezes their clouds of gas, and dense gas is where new stars form, which is why encounters so often set off bursts of star birth. Over time, pairs like this one are expected to combine into a single larger galaxy, one of the main ways galaxies grow. The pair lies in the constellation Canes Venatici.
explore: The image was obtained with the wide-field Mosaic camera of Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. North is up and east is to the left.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter telescope observed the pair through B, V, I and hydrogen-alpha filters, shown as blue, cyan, orange and red respectively.
understand.eye: The hydrogen-alpha filter isolates the glow of hydrogen gas, so the star-forming clouds stand out far more strongly than they would to the eye.

alt: A barred spiral galaxy at centre and a smaller galaxy at upper right, with bright red clouds of gas in and between them.

caption: The globular cluster M13, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter telescope at Kitt Peak
story: This image shows M13, also catalogued as NGC 6205, a giant globular cluster in the constellation Hercules. It contains several hundred thousand stars and is about 150 light-years across.
As in every globular cluster, all of M13's stars are old. Its core is so bright that many short exposures had to be taken to keep the centre from being overexposed.

A globular cluster is a dense, roughly spherical swarm of stars bound together by gravity. Because all of its stars formed at about the same time, long ago, a cluster like M13 is a natural record of our Galaxy's early history, and comparing its stars shows how stars of different masses age. The stars crowd most tightly toward the centre, which is why the core is so much brighter than the edges and so hard to photograph.
explore: The image was obtained with the wide-field Mosaic camera of Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope. It is oriented with north to the left and east at the bottom.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter telescope observed M13 through B, V and I filters, shown as blue, green and red respectively.
understand.eye: Combining many short exposures lets the image hold both the brilliant core and the faint outer stars, a range the eye cannot take in at once.

scaleExtra: M13 is about 150 light-years in diameter, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A huge, dense ball of stars that is brightest at its centre.

caption: Gamma Cassiopeiae and the nebulae IC 59 and IC 63, imaged at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center
story: The bright bluish star in this image is Gamma Cassiopeiae. It is evaporating two nearby clouds of gas, IC 59 and IC 63, whose leading edges glow strongly as they are bathed in the star's intense radiation.

Behind those glowing front lines, hints of bluish light show where some of the star's light is being scattered by the clouds. In astronomical terms, the clouds do not have long left: before long they will be scattered into the interstellar medium, the thin gas between the stars.

Hot, luminous stars pour out energetic light that can heat and strip nearby gas. The glowing edges are where that radiation strikes the clouds most directly, while the bluish haze behind them is starlight bouncing off dust, much as sunlight scatters in our own sky. Scenes like this show a star reshaping its surroundings.
explore: The image was taken in 2014 as part of the Advanced Observing Program at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center, using a 16-inch RCOS telescope with a CCD camera. It is credited to Tom Bash, John Fox and Adam Block.

understand.summary: A CCD camera on a 16-inch RCOS telescope at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center recorded the scene in visible light through B, G, R and broadband filters; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: The glowing and scattered light of these clouds is far too faint for the eye; long exposures reveal it.

alt: A bright bluish star beside two clouds of gas with glowing edges facing the star.

caption: The star cluster RMC 136, imaged by Gemini South with the GeMS adaptive optics system
story: This near-infrared image picks out individual stars inside RMC 136, a giant cluster within the Tarantula Nebula, which lies in the Large Magellanic Cloud. It was made with GeMS, the adaptive optics system on the Gemini South telescope.

RMC 136 supplies most of the energy that powers the Tarantula Nebula, lighting up its surrounding gas. The cluster's mass is estimated at about half a million times that of the Sun, which suggests it will probably turn into a globular cluster one day.

Adaptive optics corrects for the blurring caused by turbulence in Earth's atmosphere, letting a ground-based telescope separate stars that would otherwise merge into a single glow. That matters in a crowded cluster like this one. Globular clusters are dense, long-lived balls of stars, and a young, massive cluster like RMC 136 offers a rare chance to see what one may have looked like early in its life.
explore: The image is credited to the International Gemini Observatory, Robert Blum of the National Optical Astronomy Observatory, and T.A. Rector of the University of Alaska Anchorage.

understand.summary: Gemini South with the GeMS adaptive optics system observed RMC 136 in near-infrared light through J, H and Ks filters; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and adaptive optics sharpens the view well beyond what atmospheric blurring would normally allow.

alt: A dense cluster of many individual stars packed tightly together.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 55, imaged by the 0.9-meter telescope at Cerro Tololo
story: Red patches of nebulosity mark regions of active star formation in NGC 55, a nearby galaxy in this image from a 0.9-meter National Science Foundation telescope at Chile's Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory.
NGC 55 lies about five million light-years away and belongs to the Sculptor Group, a small gathering of galaxies.

The red glow in regions like these comes from hydrogen gas energised by hot, young stars that have recently formed inside the clouds, so each red patch is a sign of stellar birth. A galaxy group such as the Sculptor Group is a small collection of galaxies bound loosely together by gravity; our own Milky Way belongs to a similar gathering, the Local Group. Relatively nearby galaxies like NGC 55 are close enough that astronomers can study their star-forming regions in some detail, comparing them with those in our own Galaxy. It lies in the constellation Sculptor.
explore: The image was taken with the SMARTS 0.9-meter telescope at Cerro Tololo, using B, V and R filters together with a hydrogen-alpha filter, and was processed by T.A. Rector.

understand.summary: The 0.9-meter telescope at Cerro Tololo observed NGC 55 in visible light through B, V, R and hydrogen-alpha filters; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: The hydrogen-alpha filter isolates the glow of hydrogen gas, making star-forming regions much more prominent than they would be to the eye.

scaleExtra: NGC 55 is about five million light-years away, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A galaxy dotted with red patches of glowing gas.

caption: The globular cluster M4, imaged by the KPNO 0.9-meter telescope
story: This picture shows M4, also catalogued as NGC 6121, a globular cluster in the constellation Scorpius. It has a slightly brownish colour, and an unusual bar-like structure runs through its centre.

M4 lies about 7000 light-years away, which makes it a good candidate for the nearest globular cluster to us. It would look much brighter if not for a considerable amount of interstellar dust between us and the cluster. That same dust is responsible for its brownish tint.

Dust between the stars absorbs and scatters light, and it affects blue light more strongly than red, so objects seen through it look dimmer and redder than they really are. A globular cluster is a dense, roughly spherical swarm of old stars bound together by gravity. Being so close, M4 is a convenient place to study the individual stars of such a cluster.
explore: The picture was made using the T2KA CCD camera on the 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory in March 1995.

understand.summary: The T2KA CCD camera on the Kitt Peak 0.9-meter telescope recorded M4 in visible light; the filters and colour mapping are not published.
understand.eye: The camera's exposures gather far more light than the eye and resolve many of the cluster's individual stars.

scaleExtra: M4 is about 7000 light-years away, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A slightly brownish ball of stars with a bar-like structure through its centre.

caption: The globular cluster M53, imaged by the KPNO 0.9-meter telescope
story: This composite shows M53, also catalogued as NGC 5024, a globular cluster in the constellation Coma Berenices. The field is 14.7 arcminutes across.
M53 is an outlying globular cluster: it lies about 60000 light-years from us, and roughly the same distance from the centre of our Galaxy.

A globular cluster is a dense, roughly spherical swarm of old stars held together by gravity. Our Galaxy is surrounded by many of them, some close to its centre and others, like M53, far out in its outskirts. Because their stars formed together long ago, globular clusters act as fossils of the Milky Way's early history, and those at great distances help astronomers map the extended halo of stars that surrounds our Galaxy. The stars crowd most tightly toward the centre of the cluster, while fainter members thin out toward the edges. Comparing stars within one cluster shows how stars of different masses age.
explore: The composite was made from images taken in July 1997 with the 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory, during the Research Experiences for Undergraduates program which the National Science Foundation supports, with more images added in May 1998.

understand.summary: The 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak recorded M53 in visible light, and the images were combined into a composite; the filters and colour mapping are not published.
understand.eye: The camera's exposures gather far more light than the eye, resolving many of the cluster's stars.

scaleExtra: M53 is about 60000 light-years away, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A round, dense ball of stars that thins toward its edges.

caption: The Milky Way over the Avenue of Baobabs, Morondava, Madagascar
story: The band of the Milky Way stretches across the sky above the Avenue of Baobabs in Morondava, Madagascar, in this photograph taken in 2017. The baobab trees stand in silhouette in the foreground.
Baobabs are unusual trees, with thick, barrel-like trunks, and they are known for living a very long time. Seen against the night sky, their distinctive shapes frame the view.

The Milky Way is our own galaxy. Because we live inside its flat disc, we see it from within as a soft band of light running across the sky, made of the combined glow of countless distant stars too faint to pick out one by one. Dark lanes often seen along the band are clouds of dust that block light from the stars behind them. The band shows up most clearly where the sky is truly dark, away from city lights.
explore: The photograph was taken by Amirreza Kamkar and is shared through the IAU Office of Astronomy for Education and NOIRLab. It is also available on Zenodo.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken with a camera in visible light; the camera settings and processing are not published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers much more light than the eye, so the Milky Way looks brighter and more detailed than it would to someone standing among the trees.

alt: The band of the Milky Way stretches over barrel-trunked baobab trees silhouetted against the night sky.

caption: The Jewel Box cluster, NGC 4755, imaged by the 0.9-meter telescope at Cerro Tololo
story: The many colours of the stars in NGC 4755 are on display in this picture from the 0.9-meter telescope at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory. NGC 4755 is an open star cluster in the constellation Crux.
It is popularly known as the Jewel Box, a name that goes back to an early catalogue describing it as a superb piece of jewellery.

An open cluster is a loose group of stars that formed together from the same cloud of gas and dust. The differing colours of the stars are a clue to their nature: a star's colour reflects the temperature of its surface, with hotter stars appearing bluer and cooler stars redder. Because the members of a cluster share an age and a birthplace, differences between them mostly come down to mass, which controls how hot a star burns and how quickly it moves through its life. Heavier stars change fastest, so a cluster with stars of contrasting colours shows several stages of stellar life side by side.

understand.summary: The 0.9-meter telescope at Cerro Tololo recorded the Jewel Box in visible light; the filters and colour mapping are not published.
understand.eye: Star colours are hard to see by eye in dim light, but the camera records them, bringing out the contrasting hues of the cluster's stars.

alt: An open cluster of stars in a range of colours.
